21.7, 22.2, Total–29 (Chapter-III)
(iv) Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Government are still
awaited: Nil,  Total–Nil  (Chapter-IV)

2
CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS WHICH
HA VE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendations/Observations
2.4 The Committee notes that the overall allocation for the health sector (outside NRHM) has
been on the higher side. Still, the Committee is constrained to note that the Department has failed
to project its budgetary requirements in an effective way for the simple reason that the utilization
of funds during the Tenth Plan is far from satisfactory which is evident from the fact that the
sanctioned BE for 2005-06 and 2006-07 was Rs.4253.84 crores and Rs.3564.95 crores,
respectively, which was reduced to Rs.4096.25 crores and Rs.3433.02 crores, respectively at the
RE stage. The actual expenditure figures of Rs.2907.96 crores and Rs.3377.34 crores were even
less than the budgeted allocations at the RE stage. The Committee notes that this trend has
continued during 2007-08 also. This goes to illustrate that the Department’s record in utilization of
the allocated funds is below par. The Committee would, therefore, recommend the Department to
first ensure optimum and judicious utilization of the funds allocated instead of highlighting the
reduced budgetary allocation. The Committee also recommends to the Department to take
substantive steps so that the stumbling blocks in the utilization of sanctioned funds for 2008-09
for a crucial sector like health, are removed.
Action Taken
Noted for compliance.
Recommendations/Observations
2.7 Committee observes that in spite of its raising concerns over this trend of under utilization
of funds year after year, there does not seem to be any noticeable improvement in this regard. Time
and again the Committee has been advocating for higher allocation of funds for this sector and this
time the Committee is happy to note that the approved outlay has seen a 32% hike over the last
year’s Revised Estimate. The Committee reiterates its concern and recommends to the Department
to play a more pro-active role in identifying the problems afflicting the utilization of funds in the
Health Sector and initiate remedial measures from the very beginning of the current financial year so
that the old story of revising estimates downwards and subsequent under utilization does not recur.
Action Taken
Noted for compliance.
III. CENTRAL GOVERNMENT HEALTH SCHEME (CGHS)
Recommendations/Observations
3.3 The Committee, therefore, recommends that allocation of funds under Non-Plan be
enhanced adequately so that the services available to the CGHS beneficiaries are not affected.
2

3
Action Taken
The requirement of additional funds for Non-Plan expenditure by CGHS will be projected to the
Ministry of Finance for discussions in the Pre-Budget meeting to be taken by Secretary (Expenditure).
IV. SAFDARJUNG HOSPITAL AND V ARDHMAN MAHAVEER MEDICAL COLLEGE, NEW
DELHI
Recommendations/Observations
4.4 The Committee observes that procedures and rules are made to streamline, strengthen and
facilitate a process and not create hurdles and bottlenecks. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that effective coordination between the Department and the Hospital authorities is required in this
regard. If required, suitable steps for improvement in the procedural aspect may be initiated so as
to provide better health care delivery system.
Action Taken
In view of enhancement of powers of Additional D.G. and Medical Superintendent for
procurement of equipments to Rs.l.00 crore, the hospital is not finding difficulty in procurement
of equipments as most of the hospital equipments are below Rs.l.00 crore.
VI. ALL INDIA INSTITUTE OF MEDICAL SCIENCES (AIIMS)
Recommendations/Observations
6.2 The Committee was informed that the allocated funds would not be sufficient for
maintaining the infrastructure and patient care services of the Institute. The Committee feels that
the decrease in Non-Plan from Rs.3l0.00 crores in 2007-08 to Rs.290.00 crores is surely going
to affect the patient care services offered by the Institute. The Committee apprehends return of
the ‘user charges regime’ in AIIMS because consumables are the only negotiable component of the
Non-Plan budget as salary and bills have to be paid any way.
Action Taken
A letter has already been written to Director, AIIMS in the month of June, 2008 asking
them to workout their requirement additional funds, if any, which will be considered during
Supplementary demands.
Recommendations/Observations
6.6 The Committee would emphasize that procedural formalities for the centre should be
expedited so as to complete it by the targeted date.
Action Taken
The observation of the Committee has been noted.
Recommendations/Observations
6.9 The Committee expresses deep concern that in the premier institute of the country like
AIIMS so many posts are lying vacant. In the opinion of the Committee, this is definitely bound
to affect the quality of services rendered by the Institute. The Committee, therefore, recommends
immediate action to fill up the vacant posts.
Action Taken
All categories of vacant posts are in process of recruitment.

4
VII. POST GRADUATE INSTITUTE OF MEDICAL EDUCATION AND RESEARCH
(PGIMER), CHANDIGARH
Recommendations/Observations
7.3 The Committee is of the opinion that PGIMER is amongst India’s premier Institutes and its
developmental plans should not be affected in any way due to scarcity of funds. While
recommending that adequate funds should be made available to the PGIMER, Chandigarh to meet
its requirements for developmental works, the Committee also recommends judicious and optimum
utilization of the allocated funds.
Action Taken
The Recommendations of the Committee were/are being complied with strictly.
XI. PRADHAN MANTRI SWASTHYA SURAKSHA YOJANA (PMSSY)
Recommendations/Observations
11.6 The Committee in its 22nd Report on the Demands for Grants (2007-08) presented on
3rd May, 2007 had expressed its apprehension that it would take at least another plan period before
the six AIIMS like Institutions would start functioning in the real sense. The Committee is
constrained to modify its assessment. From the details made available to the Committee,
construction work on the Six AIIMS like Institutions is expected to start by August-
September, 2008 and would be completed in 24 months. Thus, it is more than clear now that only
buildings would be ready by the end of Eleventh Plan. The real target of making available best
health care services to public through these institutions seems to be a distant dream even now. The
Committee finds that tendering process for procurement of medical equipments is at an initial stage.
Process for other allied infrastructure facilities and manpower – both highly qualified/technical as
well as non-technical is yet so start. With regard to up gradation of 13 Medical College Institutions,
the Committee can only hope that work would be completed within the targeted date of 20 months.
The Committee is, however, worried about the fate of upgradation of Grants Medical College and
JJ hospital, Mumbai due to a court case pending in Nagpur High Court in the matter. The
Committee is of the view that the Department should take up other linked activities like arranging
for the faculty and requisite infrastructure simultaneously so that no delay takes place in
operationalization of the Institutions once the construction activity is completed.
Action Taken
Noted. The civil construction work is likely to be completed by the end of 2010. However,
parallel activities for procurement of medical equipment, manpower planning and recruitment,
finalization of governance and management structure as also preparation of curriculum design have
been initiated in 2008. The effort will be to make the hospital functional by the end of 2010 and
Medical College operational by academic year 2011.
Recommendations/Observations
11.7 The Committee also recommends that funds as and when required should be made available
to the Department. The Committee would, however, like to point out that though funds have never
been a problem for this ambitious project of national importance, utilization thereof has been far
from satisfactory level. The Committee, accordingly, recommends setting up of a joint mechanism
of Centre and the concerned States so that greater coordination is achieved and effective
monitoring of the ongoing projects is done. The Committee also calls for greater emphasis on
adhering to the time lines so that the overall cost of the project is not escalated further.

5
Action Taken
All out efforts are being made to fully utilize the funds allocated for the Project. A
Committee under the Chairmanship of Chief Secretaries of the concerned States is being set up to
monitor the progress of setting up of each of the six AIIMS-like institutions.
XII. IMPROVEMENT OF NURSING SERVICES
Recommendations/Observations
12.4 The Committee is not aware about the existence of any Monitoring Committee for such
projects. The Committee is of the view that such a mechanism will prove to be very useful,
especially in view of Rs.198.00 crores allocated for strengthening/upgradation of Nursing Services.
The Committee welcomes the enhancement in the assistance to be provided to Nursing
Institutions from Rs.10.00 lakhs to Rs.25.00 lakhs. Such a move was overdue. The Committee,
however, wonders whether any exercise has been initiated for identification of locations of all the
proposed Centres/Schools/Colleges so far. The Committee would appreciate if implementation of all
these projects is carried out in a time-bound manner. The Committee is not aware about any
assessment/review made recently about the (training both pre and in-service) programmes for
Nurses and also functioning of Training Institutions for Nurses. The Committee is of the view that
such an exercise is necessary for strengthening the Nursing Services which is a very crucial
component of health care.
Action Taken
Noted for compliance. The establishment of Monitoring and Evaluation Cell has been
proposed in the EFC Memo. Although no assessment has been made recently for pre and in-service
training and that of Training Institutions for Nurses but it is envisaged that the Monitoring and
Evaluation Cell when set up would take care of these aspects.
The enhanced grant of Rs.25.00 lakhs is meant for procurement of A.V. AIDS, laboratory
equipment, furniture, library, transport etc. and is need based and would be released to the nursing
institutions on the basis of proposals to be received from the states. Locations for establishing
Centres/Schools/Colleges have been identified. Details are at Annexure-XI.
Recommendations/Observations
12.5 The Committee is happy to note that the National Awards for Nurses, given as a mark of
highest recognition for the meritorious services of the nurses and nursing profession in the
Country, that continued up to 1989, have been revived and named as the National Florence
Nightingale Award from 2007 with the consent of the President of India. 17 Nursing personnel
have been awarded with this prestigious award during the year 2007.
Action Taken
The National Florence Nightingale Awards for the year 2008 have also been distributed by
the President of India to 26 meritorious nursing personnel in the award ceremony held on
12.5.2008 at Rashtrapati Bhavan.
Recommendations/Observations
12.6 The Committee recommends that a suitable mechanism should be evolved for maintaining
a live register of nurses so as to enable the Department for formulating appropriate policy
pertaining to nurses.

6
Action Taken
The Indian Nursing Council is already seized of the matter and will make efforts to devise
suitable mechanism to overcome the problem.
Recommendations/Observations
12.7 The Committee recommends that the Department should make all out efforts including
effective co-ordination and close monitoring so that all the proposals for strengthening of nursing
education are implemented properly and desired results are achieved for getting adequate number
of qualified and trained nursing personnel.
Action Taken
As regards effective coordination and monitoring of the project the Monitoring and
Evaluation Cell as explained in para 12.4 would take care of this aspect.
XV. NATIONAL URBAN HEALTH MISSION (NUHM)
Recommendations/Observations
15.4 The Committee observes that NUHM is one of the most ambitious Projects after National
Rural Health Mission (NRHM). Objectives of the Mission are laudable and are according to the
requirements of the present scenario. The Committee cautions the Department to take all necessary
steps so that the problems afflicting the implementation of NRHM like those related to ground level
healthcare functionaries, availability of doctors, paramedics and infrastructure do not recur and
interfere in the implementation of this parallel scheme meant for urban areas. For achieving the
targets proposed under mission, the Department should do proper homework and work out
modalities for their implementation. The Department should start coordinating with the States right
from the beginning of the project. The Committee would like to be apprised about the progress
made in this regard.
Action Taken
Based on the document on NUHM approved by Minister of Health and Family Welfare, a
draft EFC Memo for NUHM has been circulated to the concerned Ministries for seeking their view/
comments.
The EFC proposal envisages to achieve the objectives of NUHM by strengthening the
extents primary public health systems, rationalising the available manpower and resources, filling
the gaps in service delivery through private partnership through a regulatory frame work and also
through a communitised risk pooling/insurance mechanism with IT enablement, capacity building of
key stake holders and by making special provision for inclusion of the most vulnerable amongst
the poor.
All the State/UT Governments have been requested to start the work of GIS mapping of
the selected cities in TOP PRIORITY basis.
The teams of this Ministry has visited the States of Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh
Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Jharkhand, Chandigarh UT, Haryana, Punjab, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal,
Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand. A presentation on proposed NUHM and the GIS mapping was arranged
and the discussion was also held on various issues pertaining to the NUHM. The officials of
Puducherry were requested to come at Chennai and the officials of A&N Islands were requested
to come at Kolkata to participate in the meeting.

7
The teams would visit other States/UT Governments soon.
XVII. NATIONAL CANCER CONTROL PROGRAMME (NCCP)
Recommendations/Observations
17.9 The Committee recommends to the Department to give utmost priority to evaluation of the
National Cancer Control Programme by a premier agency having experience of work in such
Disease Control Programmes. Proper evaluation would help in identifying weak links and result in
effective implementation of various components of the programme.
Action Taken
This Ministry is inserting an advertisement through DA VP in leading dailies relating to
evaluation of the NCCP (Enquiry for Expression of Interest). This will attract more organizations
in evaluation of the scheme. Efforts will be taken to complete the exercise of the evaluation within
the stipulated time-frame.
XVIII. NATIONAL TOBACCO CONTROL PROGRAMME (NTCP)
Recommendations/Observations
18.4 The Committee was informed last year that the ‘in principle’ approval of the Planning
Commission for setting up of the National Regulatory Authority and Referral Labs for testing Tar
and Nicotine content in various tobacco products has been obtained. Process for seeking approval
of the competent authority had already begun at that time. The Committee, however, notes that no
progress seems to have been made in this regard thereafter. Keeping in view the prolonged process
of getting the approval of the competent authority, the Committee does not have much hope about
the same being obtained by June, 2008. The Department has to make concerted efforts so that
approval of the competent authority for setting up of the National Regulatory Authority, backbone
of the entire programme, is obtained at the earliest.
Action Taken
The Ministry has noted the recommendation for compliance and further necessary action.
Recommendations/Observations
18.5 More than one million people are dying due to consumption of tobacco in the country. The
Committee, therefore, strongly feels that the Ministry needs to bring up sustained Mass Media/IEC
campaign regarding the adverse and harmful effects of tobacco consumption immediately, as also
when NTCP is launched. Sufficient funds should be made available for the same.
Action Taken
The Ministry has noted the recommendation for compliance and further necessary action.
XX. NATIONAL PROGRAMME FOR PREVENTION AND CONTROL OF DIABETES,
CARDIOV ASCULAR DISEASES STROKE (NPDCS)
Recommendations/Observations
20.4 The Committee is happy to note that the pilot phase of the programme has finally taken off
during 2007-08.

8
Action Taken
The budget allocation for 2008-09 is only for Rs.30 crores. In view of this provision the
new districts to be covered in 2008-09 will be 25. State NCD Cells are to be set up in 25 States
and 1 dedicated unit of Cardiovascular Disease/diabetes/stroke Prevention is proposed to be set up.
Recommendations/Observations
20.5 The Committee notes that out of an approved outlay of Rs.1660.50 crores for the Eleventh
Five Year Plan, only Rs.30.00 crores have been earmarked for 2008-09. This, when taken into
account along with last year’s utilization of Rs.4.42 crores, leaves behind a whooping amount of
Rs.1625.50 crores for the last three years of the plan. The Committee is given to understand that
a steering Committee has been established to review and expedite the Programme. A meeting of the
States participating in the pilot project was held on 17th October, 2007. Appreciating this initiative,
the Committee recommends to the Department to carry forward the programme vigorously during
the remaining period of the Plan so that the set targets are achieved with the optimum utilization
of funds available for the programme.
Action Taken
The recommendations of the Committee have been noted and all out efforts would be made
to comply with the same.
XXI. MEDICAL EDUCATION
Recommendations/Observations
21.4 The Committee is aware that keeping in view the shortage of doctors and existing medical
institutions not being adequate enough, MCI norms for opening of colleges/increase of seats need
to be reviewed. The Committee, however, feels that this exercise should be undertaken with
extreme caution so that objective of imparting quality medical education remains intact. Relaxing
norms by allowing private promoters to have land in two pieces within 10 Kms. of each other and
allowing corporate entities to setup medical colleges are initiatives which should be implemented
after examining all pros and cons. The Committee is of the opinion that in the exercise of relaxation

due weightage.

The observations of the Committee will be kept in view while finalizing the regulations of
MCI.
Recommendations/Observations
21.5 The Committee also takes note of the suggestion of the Department to MCI for relaxing
the age of retirement of staff of Private Medical Educational Institutes from 65 to 70 years, subject
to their physical ability, in order to fill-up the acute shortage of teaching staff in that sector.
Secretary, Department of Health and Family Welfare has also informed the Committee that a

9

Action Taken
As per the existing guidelines, only one time assistance can be provided to the Institute
irrespective of the cost of the equipment. As per the present condition, Rs.3.00 crore is the

XIX. NA TIONAL MENTAL HEALTH PROGRAMME (NMHP)
Recommendations/Observations
19.4 The Committee is constrained to note that in spite of approved outlay being drastically
reduced to nearly half for the National Mental Health Programme, the expenditure reported upto

33
29th February, 2008 is a meagre 14.13 crores. A proposal for releasing funds to the extent of

According to the Tenth Plan Scheme of the National Mental Health Programme, all the
proposals for extending District Mental Health Programme, Upgradation of Psychiatric Wings of
Government Medical Colleges/General Hospitals and Modernisation of Government Mental Hospitals

consideration. These proposals are first examined by a Working Group and the recommendations

Secretary (Health and FW) for approval. Besides, approval of IFD is also obtained in the matter.
The proposals not recommended by the Working Group are got corrected by the State
Governments/Institutions. Non-receipt of adequate number of complete proposals in time from the
State Governments leads to lesser release of grant-in-aid and consequently under utilization of
Budget allocation of the National Mental Health Programme.
For effective and efficient implementation of the programme, periodical interactions with the
State Governments have been held. A review meeting on NMHP with the State Health Secretaries/
Directors of Health Services/Nodal Officers was held in February, 2007. A meeting was also held
with the Health Secretaries of States in July, 2007 in which implementation of NMHP was, inter
alia, discussed. Regional Meetings were held during August-September, 2007 with the State Nodal
Officers for NMHP to review progress of implementation of the Programme. Review meetings on
the implementation of NMHP were also held on 3rd March and 25th March, 2008. All the
representatives of State Governments were requested to submit proposals for assistance under
various components of the Programme and to submit financial year-wise Utilisation Certificates
along with Audited Statements
In order to overcome these problems, it has been envisaged in the EFC Proposal on NMHP
for implementation during the Eleventh  Five Year Plan, to decentralize the programme and also to
integrate it with National Rural Health Mission. Grants under different schemes to a particular State
would be released through the State Health Society along with the schemes and guidelines for
NMHP. S tate Nodal Of ficer representing the programme in the State Health Society would get the
grants released for various districts and institutions. At the district level, the Programme Officer
would represent the programme in the District Health Society and facilitate operationalisation of
DMHP.
A proposal for releasing funds to the extent of Rs.22.165 crore through the State Health
Societies was under consideration but this could not materialize, as the I.F.D./competent authority
did not approve the proposal, pending the approval of the EFC Proposal on NMHP for
implementation during the Eleventh  Five Year Plan.
Recommendations/Observations
19.6 Committee is dismayed at the fact that the expansion of the National Mental Health
programme envisaged for the Eleventh Plan is yet to be approved. The Committee recommends to
the Department to present its case strongly and effectively so as to get necessary approval without
further delay. Further, the Department can not simply shy away from its responsibility by stating
that progress of the events in these scheme depends on the active cooperation of the State
Governments and other stake holders. The Committee, accordingly, recommends the Department to

34
problem areas which need to be addressed. The Department should be proactive so as to motivate

The EFC Proposal on NMHP for implementation during the Eleventh Five Year Plan has
been circulated among the appraisal agencies i.e.  Department of Expenditure and Planning
Commission. The proposal will be taken up for approval of the Expenditure finance Committee
soon.
For effective and efficient implementation of the programme, periodical interactions with the
State Governments have been held. A review meeting on NMHP with the State Health Secretaries/
Directors of Health Services/Nodal Officers was held in February, 2007. A meeting was also held
with the Health Secretaries of States in July, 2007 in which implementation of NMHP was, inter
alia, discussed. Regional Meetings were held during August-September, 2007 with the State Nodal
Officers for NMHP to review progress of implementation of the Programme. Review meetings on

The Committee would like to emphasize that all the districts need to be covered at the

It has been envisaged in the EFC Proposal on NMHP for implementation during the Eleventh

XXIII. NEW SCHEMES
Recommendations/Observations
23.2 The Committee is dismayed to note that every year the Department announces new
schemes/programmes, many of which are without finalizing the modalities and proper ground work,
thereby resulting in under or no utilization of funds. The Committee recommends to the Department
to enhance its efforts to complete all necessary formalities and launch the programmes at the

Action Taken
Most of the Schemes were introduced during 2007-08 It being the first year for
implementation, there was slow progress in appraisal/approval of the schemes which slowed down
the pace of expenditure. The implementation process has gradually gained momentum and the
progress in this regard for certain schemes is given as follows:—
• Pilot project on Prevention and Control of Human Rabies.
• Leptospirosis Control Programme.
The two projects, initially envisaged for five years have been revised in consultation with
Integrated Finance Division and approval of the competent authority has now been obtained to
carry out the projects on pilot basis for two years only.
Project on Prevention and Control of Human Rabies is being carried out on pilot basis in
four cities, namely Delhi, Ahmedabad, Bangalore and Pune, whereas Leptospirosis Control

material.

at an advanced stage of formulation. The programme is to be proceeded by
amendments in the THOA Acts and Rules. The amended rules have been notified. The

• Oral Health – While the Ministry has been in the process of preparing an EFC proposal
for the programme, the Ministry of Finance issued instructions in June, 2008 to the
effect that no new scheme/programme should be launched in the current financial year
even if Budget provision has been made for the same unless it has been mentioned in

36
the Finance Minister’s Budget Speech for 2008-09. As this programme was not

Nevertheless, in the meeting of Senior Officers under the chairmanship of Secretary

XXIV. MISCELLANEOUS
Recommendations/Observations
24.2 The Committee recommends the Department to work out modalities for establishing
specialized kidney centers immediately and in the mean time approach the Planning Commission for
funds with a proposal to improve dialysis facility in the country. In view of increasing gap in
demand and supply, at least the well known Institutes across India should be provided with the
dialysis machines during the current financial year. The Committee would like to be informed about
the steps taken by the Department in this regard.
Action Taken
There is shortage of Dialysis facilities in the country. Health is state subject and it is for
state Government concerned to provide the health care facilities to the general public. There is
shortage of qualified doctors to run the dialysis machines. There are very few centres which are
providing D.M. (Nephrology) super specialty courses and there are about 500 such specialities in
the country. Curriculum for training of physicians for dialysis is being finalised in collaboration with
IGNOU with a view to start short term training programmes to bridge the gap. Efforts are being
made to initiate the standalone dialysis in the CGHS Delhi. In this regard, some proposals are under
consideration and expert opinion has been taken. Till such time, CGHS patients are reimbursed the
money spent by beneficiaries on Dialysis in the private sector. Similarly other organised sector and

37
Government employees who are covered under similar insurance schemes namely CS (MA) and
ESI are provided the reimbursement.
Central Government institutions e.g. AIIMS, PGI, JIPMER, RML Hospital and Safdarjung
Hospital are already having Dialysis facilities and further upgradation is done from time to time.
There is decentralised decision making in the Health Care Delivery System under National Rural
Health System and State Governments can require equipments themselves.
National Organ Transplant Programme is being finalised and likely to be initiated soon.

III. CENTRAL GOVERNMENT HEALTH SCHEME (CGHS)
Recommendations/Observations
3.5 The Committee would like to point out that situation is some what different. Problems are
being faced both by the CGHS functionaries and beneficiaries. Technicians, Junior staff manning
counters in dispensaries and attending doctors need to be fully trained. Practical problems like
internet and electricity failure have to be tackled by having an alternative arrangement. These initial
teething problems should not be allowed to be prolonged. At present, beneficiaries which include
senior citizens also are being made to wait for hours at the dispensaries. Their ordeal starts right
from the registration counter and continues upto delivery of medicines. The Committee would
appreciate if all the measures including training, smooth running of computers with full
connectivity, backup for power failure are taken at the earliest and also closely monitored.
Action Taken
The Speed of Internet has improved w.e.f. 1st April 2008. After discussing with MTNL
Internet speed has been enhanced to 2mbps at dispensaries with effect from 1.4.2008.
NIC has also strengthened the Computer servers to improve better connectivity. The
support of Data Entry Operators at Dispensaries is continuing. MTNL has identified Nodal officers
specifically to address the internet related complaints of CGHS dispensaries. NIC has also
earmarked eight Supervisors to take care of software related problems at dispensaries. The project
is closely monitored by Additional Directors, CGHS, Director, CGHS, Sr. Technical Director, NIC
and Senior Officers of Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. In addition regular meetings are held
with officials of MTNL.
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
The Committee had called for taking measures which includes training of the staff,
connectivity of the computer systems and their backup for power failure. However, the
Department has concentrated on the aspect of internet related issues, viz., enhancing its
speed and software related problems. The issue of training of staff and the power backup
seems to have been ignored at this juncture. The Committee would like to emphasize that
though internet efficiency is a vital aspect of the computerization programme, yet it has to
be seen in totality. The issue of proper training of the staff and the power backup are also
crucial for the success of the computerization exercise. The Committee, therefore, expects
the Department to chalk out a proper strategy in this regard.
Recommendations/Observations
3.6 The Committee has been emphasizing for long for introduction of two shift system in
CGHS. The Committee does not appreciate the contention of the Ministry that a large number of
private hospitals and diagnostic centres have been empanelled under the CGHS and in case of
emergency, beneficiaries can go there for treatment and claim re-imbursement later. The Committee
would like to draw the attention of the Ministry once again to the fact that idea behind having two
shifts in CGGS dispensaries is the inconvenience being faced by the CGHS beneficiaries, majority
of them office goers in going to the dispensaries in the morning hours. The Committee is disturbed

42
by the element of helplessness shown by the Ministry in their candid admission of staff side
vehemently opposing the move. In this era where the service providers like banks etc. are opting
for flexible timings to give their customers maximum possible services, at least the Ministry could
have come forward with a positive and proactive approach. The Committee would reiterate its
recommendation made last year for starting two shifts in a few dispensaries as a test case. One
must not forget that CGHS is a service oriented scheme, supposedly providing health care mainly
to our serving employees and pensioners. It is the responsibility of the Ministry to make the CGHS
employees understand and not to be pressurized by them.
Action Taken
The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare intends to take the matter before the Committee
of Secretaries.
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
The Committee observes that its recommendation regarding starting of two shifts
system in CGHS dispensaries has ultimately resulted in a positive response from the
Department. The Committee would appreciate if the matter is placed before the Committee
of Secretaries at the earliest.
Recommendations/Observations
3.7 The Committee recommends that construction of dispensary in Dwarka where land is
already available should start at the earliest. All procedural formalities should be expedited and
completion of project strictly monitored.

In view of the increase in the number of CGHS beneficiaries (serving/retired) and their
dependants in the sub city of Dwarka, the competent authority accorded approval for relocation
of CGHS dispensary in Dwarka in lieu  of closure of Moti Nagar dispensary, where the daily

adjusted in nearby dispensaries.

awaited.
Presently no suitable accommodation is available for housing CGHS Dispensary in Dwarka.
However, efforts are continuing for locating suitable accommodation in Dwarka for the opening of
a dispensary at Dwarka.
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
The Committee was given to understand that land for CGHS dispensary was available
in Dwarka. The Department has in its recent update had admitted that it had been allotted
three plots of land in Dwarka at Sectors 6, 8 and 12. The problem cited here is that the
construction work of a dispensary could not be started for want of a formal possession of
the plots being given by the DDA to the Department. The Committee has been apprised that
reminders have been sent to the DDA and their reply is still awaited. The Committee is

43
providing possession of the plots in Dwarka when the same had already been allotted. It is

III. INFRASTRUCTURE STRENGTHENING
Recommendations/Observations
3.1 NRHM aims at strengthening of Primary Health Infrastructure and improving effective
service delivery across the country. Sub-centres, Primary Healthcare Centres and Community
Health Centres are the three pillars on which rural infrastructure is built. As on March, 2007, there
are 1,45,272 Sub-Centres, 22,370 PHCs and 4045 CHCs in the country. There is a shortfall of
20,855 Sub-Centres, 6491 PHCs and 2525 CHCs in the country based on the 2001 population
norms. The Committee has been constantly drawing the attention of the Department to the uneven
spread of these centres across the country with prominent gaps in the High Focus States. The
Committee finds that there is no marked improvement in this regard.
The Committee has been expressing its serious concern on the continuance of lack of rural
health infrastructure, especially in the High Focus States where the need is the most. On being
asked to identify the problem areas, the Committee has been informed that health infrastructure and
allocation of health workers under NRHM is planned on the population, work load and distance
norms. Shortages on the basis of 2001 population are quantified as the difference between the
required number of facilities/providers as per the norms and those that are functioning or in
position. This method of determining norms and shortage does not take into account the varying
epidemiological, geographical and socio-demographic patterns across the different States/
communities and between rural and urban areas within States. The actual availability of different
types of providers or the extent of private/voluntary sector involvement in healthcare delivery at
the community level is also not taken into account. The Committee notes that against the backdrop
of these very visible deficiencies, norms for setting up of the Sub-Centres and PHCs have been
modified by the Steering Committee of the Planning Commission. These norms to be adopted
during the Eleventh Plan have been duly approved by the Planning Commission also. The
Committee has been given to understand that population-centric norms are replaced with flexible
norms comprising habitation-based needs, community based needs and disease-pattern based needs.
Action Taken
The core objective of the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) is to strengthen primary
healthcare infrastructure for effective service delivery especially in the rural areas. Acknowledging
the limitation of a population centric norm, NRHM has provided for construction of health facilities
based on caseload, distance and other criterions. Construction of Sub-Centres, PHC, CHC etc. have
been taken up from NRHM funds as well as Finance Commission funds released to States. The
suggestion of the Planning Commission has also been taken cognizance of by the Ministry.
V. NATIONAL T.B. CONTROL PROGRAMME
Recommendations/Observations
5.4 The Committee appreciates the successful implementation of RNTCP Phase-I and ongoing
Phase-II. Several initiatives/interventions taken at different levels and variety of implementing
64

65
agencies have contributed to the increasing population coverage and 85% cure rate. However, India
still contributes 20% of TB cases reported in the world. Out of 8.8 million cases per annum, 1.8
million cases are from India alone. New complex offshoots of TB also keep on emerging, the most
visible being worsening HIV epidemic increasing the number of TB cases. The Committee notes
that HIV is the most potent risk factor for progression of TB infection to disease form HIV-TB
patients detected in 2005 were 12,062, 13,614 in 2006 and 18,559 in 2007. The Committee is
aware that increase in number of co-infected (HIV–TB) patients being detected over the last three
years is a result of innovative and coordinated measures taken by the Department. But the other
dimension of this trend is increasing complexities involved in the treatment of such cases. The
Committee hopes that the National Framework formulated by RNTCP and NACP for joint TB/HIV
collaborative activities will lead to better and effective control of this emerging problem area.
Action Taken
With increasing number of HIV infected TB patients being routinely detected by the
cross-referral mechanisms between RNTCP and NACP, the programmes have prioritized providing
access to HIV care to the co-infected patients.
The Central TB Division, in collaboration with NACO, has successfully piloted a mechanism
for decentralized delivery of CPT to HIV infected TB patients through RNTCP and referral of all
such cases to nearest NACP ART Centre, where these patients would be promptly provided
monthly supplies of ART. These interventions have been included in the National framework for
joint TB/HIV collaborative activities and would be implemented in the country in a phased manner.
Recommendations/Observations
5.5 The Committee observes that the other major challenge to TB control in the country is
increasing number of MDR-TB cases. The Committee is aware that such cases are bound to
increase the magnitude and severity of TB epidemic and pose a major threat to TB control. The
Committee in its earlier Report has pointed out that 7% defaulters in a year is quite a significant
number of cases remaining untreated or half-treated. With a single TB patient infecting 10-15
persons in a year, rate of infection is bound to increase. The Committee would like to point out
that formulation of guidelines for management of MDR-TB cases and publication thereof will not
prove to be sufficient. The Committee had given a simple suggestion for identifying the defaulter
TB patients from the records being maintained at centres/hospitals with the help of NGOs/Social
Workers and Private Practitioners. Intention of the Committee was to identify such cases at the
first default stage itself. The Committee finds that under a new initiative a total of 50 MDR-TB
patients were to be registered for treatment in Gujarat and Maharashtra during 2007-08 and to be
doubled every year subsequently and ultimately in the entire country. While welcoming this
initiative, the Committee would also like to point out that cost of MDR-TB treatment is 300 times
more than non-MDR TB. The Committee can only say that preventive measures will be both cost-
effective and helpful for the patients. The Committee is of the firm opinion that through effective
IEC activities and alertness of health workers, regular intake of medicines can be easily monitored.
The Committee, therefore, suggests that in monitoring of TB patients the most vital aspect should
not be ignored at any cost.
Action Taken
The Ministry agrees with the observation of the Committee that measures to prevent the
development of MDR-TB will be both cost-effective and helpful for the patients. In consonance
with this spirit, the key focus of the programme is to make sure that the patients complete their
treatment as per schedule and on default the retrieval actions are taken immediately. Thus emphasis

66
of the programme is to implement quality DOTS to achieve highest cure rates and prevent MDR
TB.
The programme is laying lot of stress on ensuring provision of anti-TB drugs under the
direct observation. This aspect is covered during the modular training as well as reinforced during
supervisory visits and also during internal evaluations.
The RNTCP views management of MDR TB as a ‘standard of care’ issue and has identified
the following challenges and is addressing them on a priority basis:
• Minimizing default from treatment.
• Ensuring accurate categorization of previously treated patients as Category-II.
• Ensuring reliable DOT throughout treatment.
• Improve re-treatment success through intensified support, supervision, and monitoring
of DOT in category II patients through involvement of NGOs, PPs and Community
V olunteers.
• Improving Public-Private Mix (PPM) activities and uptake of DOTS by private sector
and medical colleges.
The Ministry agrees with the views of the Committee and focuses its highest priority to
reduce the default among TB patients through constant monitoring, involvement of NGOs, other
sectors and creating awareness through IEC activities.

Recommendations/Observations
7.5 As per the existing scheme under the Programme, the NGOs perform cataract operations
directly under the supervision of Respective District Blindness Control Societies, which function
under the State Blindness Control Society at the State level. To a query regarding the monitoring
of the working of 881 NGO hospitals with eye-care facilities spread over in different parts of the
country, the Committee has been informed that working of NGO hospitals with eye care facilities
participating under NPCB are being monitored by the respective District Blindness Control Societies
directly. However, during State level meetings organized under the programme, NGOs’ hospitals are
also invited and the work done by them is reviewed. In addition, general guidelines for pre-
operative, operative and post-operative precautions for eye surgery have been circulated to all
States from time to time and last time these were circulated in the year 2007-08 to avoid eye
mishaps.
The Committee has been taking note of instances of malfunctioning of Eye Camps reported
in the Media from across the different States. The Committee feels that monitoring of Eye Camps
is being exclusively done by the District Blindness Control Societies. Department’s role starts as
and when reports regarding malfunctioning of Eye Camps held in States are brought to the notice
of the Ministry. Corrective measures are accordingly taken by the Ministry. The Committee,
however, feels that the Department needs to be more pro-active in such cases. One corrective
measure which can be initiated by the Department without any special efforts involved is to review

68
the performance of such Eye Camps in the State level meetings, with required follow-up action
taken on the reported incidents of malfunctioning of Eye Camps. The Committee is also of the
view that follow-up treatment after Eye Camps should be made mandatory and strictly enforced.
District hospital authorities also need to be involved in the conducting of such Eye Camps by
introduction of compulsory pre-checks in Eye Camps before start of Eye surgery and other
treatment. The Committee would like to add here that the Department should also devise some
method of surprise inspection of eye camps organized by the NGOs to facilitate cataract
operations. This, the Committee feels would ensure stricter compliance by all the concerned entities
and help reduce eye mishaps. The Committee notes that the process for independent evaluation of
NPCB including evaluation of work being done by NGOs has been initiated. The Committee would
appreciate if this exercise is expedited so that corrective measures are taken.
Action Taken
The National Programme for Control of Blindness (NPCB) has been circulating guidelines
on “Pre-operative, Operative and Post-Operative precautions for Eye Surgery” to States for further
dissemination to all State level hospitals, Medical Colleges, Regional Institutes of Ophthalmology and
NGO hospitals from time to time to avoid eye mishaps. As a follow up action, State Governments
are being directed separately to ensure that these guidelines are strictly followed in all eye care
facilities and Eye Screening Camps in their States. It has also been proposed to make it mandatory
for the State Governments to obtain an undertaking regarding strict compliance of the guidelines
from the organizers before granting permission to them for conducting Eye Screening Camps.
Now, Eye Screening Camps are allowed but the Eye operations in the camps have been banned
by Government of India due to high rate of mishaps in such camps w.e.f. 1997.
Recommendations/Observations
7.9 The Committee’s attention has also been drawn to the findings of a survey on Rapid
Assessment of TRACHOMA cases done in the district of Haryana, Gujarat, U.P., Uttarakhand,
Punjab and Rajasthan. Findings of this survey were that against the popular perception of there
being no transmission of trachoma cases in India, all districts showed active cases.
The Committee notes with disappointment that the target to bring prevalence of blindness to
0.8% by 2007 has not been reached. The Department has informed that as per the report of Rapid
Survey on Avoidable Blindness (2007), the prevalence of blindness has come down to 1% and that
Cataract remains the single largest cause of blindness, low vision and one eye blindness in India. The
Committee also infers from the above study that the prevalence of blindness due to Trachoma also
continues to be there. It is a well known fact that blindness is a bane of nature. The Committee
believes that most of the people in smaller towns and rural areas are not aware of the symptoms
of the above ailments, and the methods to manage eye care, hence their eye-care service seeking
behavior pattern do not change. The Committee exhorts the Department to take all possible necessary
steps to devise IEC activities in local media and television channels so that awareness among the
people is increased. The Committee believes a lot of cases of blindness can be checked by such a
measure and would in the long run help to achieve the targeted goals under the programme.
Action Taken
On the basis of findings of the Survey on Rapid Assessment of TRACHOMA about
presence of Trachoma cases in some pockets of some States in the country, IEC activities for
public awareness about Trachoma have been intensified through electronic media such as Radio,
Television, print and press media etc. The guidelines in this regard have also been issued to States
including NE States. Spots on TV and Radio have been produced in regional languages also.

Recommendations/Observations
3.2 The Committee welcomes the modification in the criteria for assessing the requirement of

realities. The Committee is also of the view that change in the norms for health infrastructure
proposed by the Planning Commission was called for. The Committee is, however, not aware
whether any preparatory exercise has been initiated for conducting surveys as per the revised
norms. The Committee is afraid that if this issue is allowed to linger on for long, the very objective
of NRHM of bridging gaps in the health care will continue to be a distant dream. The Committee,
accordingly, impresses upon the Department to initiate action at the earliest.

of the need based projection for construction of facilities as proposed by the States in their State
Programme Implementation Plans (PIPs) while evaluating their Plans. Approvals are based on the
extant and future capacity for manpower augmentation in the States so that the expansion does not

Recommendations/Observations
5.9 Committee’s attention has also been drawn by Studies like Social Assessment Study,
Institutional Assessment Study in respect of TB Control measures undertaken so far. The Committee
would like to point out that TB infection is no more confined to the poor and marginalized sections
of the society. Growing number of patients now belong to middle class and also affluent population.
There is an urgent need for making an analysis of basic factors behind this emerging situation which
can ultimately reach to alarming proportions. The Committee hopes that with the availability of both
funds and manpower, the Department will take up such an exercise at the earliest.
Action Taken
Survey undertaken by TB Research Centre, Chennai (TRC) has shown that the prevalence
of TB is around 4 times higher amongst the lower socio-economic strata as compared to the
higher. However, TB being an airborne infection, can affect individuals from any of the socio-
economic groups. Studies indicate that some of the other key predisposing factors, besides
overcrowding and malnutrition, include smoking, diabetes, HIV co-infection etc. which cut across
all the socio-economic groups. The most effective way to achieve TB control is to cut the
transmission of infection by early diagnosis and prompt treatment of all TB patients. The
programme is hence focusing on providing quality assured diagnostic and treatment services which
are easily accessible to all the sections of the community. The programme has plans to repeat the
social assessment study during the current phase of RNTCP project wherein some of these factors
would be evaluated.

ASHA
Recommendations/Observations
3.12 Capacity building of ASHA is critical in enhancing her effectiveness as a link between the
community and the health facility. The initial orientation training is for a period of 23 days spread
in 5 rounds over a period of 12 months and followed by periodic re-training for about 2 days once
every alternate month, apart from the on-the-job training she would be getting. Training modules
for this purpose have been developed based on a thematic approach and States have also

90
constituted district and block training teams for this purpose. The Department has informed the
Committee, during its discussion on demand for grants, that selection of 5,87,512 ASHA has been
completed, 4,90,000 ASHA have completed their first round training and 2,18,339 ASHA have been
provided with drug kits.
The Committee is happy to note the progress made by the Department on the ASHA
initiative under NRHM. It is also happy to note that 86.41 % ASHA have been trained in their first
module post induction training till 12th March, 2008. The Committee observes that ASHAs have to
undergo three more rounds of training. So far, only 27% ASHAs have undergone 2nd round of
training. The Committee is of the view that every effort needs to be made to ensure that second
round of training of all the ASHAs is completed at the earliest.
The Committee has its apprehensions regarding the effectivity of ASHA as a multipurpose
social health activist, as envisaged under the NRHM. The Committee observes that job
responsibilities of ASHA are manifold as indicated below:—
– Awareness generation - Health, RCH, HIV/AIDS.
– Advising newly married couples for their special needs.
– Guiding pregnant women for availing of institutional facilities for Anti-Natal, Natal and
Post-Natal needs.
– Counselling on nutrition, pregnancy, breast-feeding, immunization and family planning.
– Establishing  link with PHCs, private providers and others for service requirement of
beneficiaries.
– Mobilizing parents for child survival interventions.
– Promoting basic sanitization.
– Provision of non-clinical spacing contraceptives.
– Surveillance of communicable diseases.
Action Taken
Training under various modules is at different stages in the States. The second module
training is complete in Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh and Uttarakhand. In Orissa and Uttar
Pradesh 2nd, 3rd and 4th modules have been combined and the training is on. It will be complete
by September, 2008 in Orissa. In Bihar also 2nd, 3rd and 4th modules are being combined and
training is to commence soon as training of Trainers is complete.
State facilitators have been deputed in Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, Uttarakhand and
NE States to facilitate the training programme.
ASHAs are performing various tasks. National Health System Resource Centre (NHSRC) is
reviewing the ‘job responsib ilities’ and “Role clarity of ASHA”.
Recommendations/Observations
3.13 ASHA is also the primary provider for National Health Programme. She is the Depot Holder
for health commodities like Vitamin A. Impregnated bed nets. ORS etc. She is also supposed to
handle treatment of minor ailments. Another major task assigned to ASHA is to provide escort
services for women seeking delivery services at institutions, requiring emergency care and MTP
services, women and men for clinical contraception services and VCTC. The Committee has been

91
given to understand that States have also taken up the training of ASHAs on diagnosis of malaria
cases. For being eligible for ASHA. a woman has to be 25 to 35 years of age, married, resident
of the village, acceptable to the village and community and proficient in reading and writing. The
Committee fails to understand as to how a single woman, who is a simple villager, can take care
of one thousand population by performing such wide-ranging tasks. Situation becomes more
complex and well away from ground realities when one finds that only remuneration payable to
ASHA is for providing Escort Services. Instances of Escort Services may not be very frequent
some times. The Committee strongly feels that ASHA is supposed to play a very challenging role.
Action Taken
ASHA is already performing wide ranging tasks for which incentives are being given. The
list of remuneration and activities is at Annexure-V.
Recommendations/Observations
3.14 The Committee is of the view that with the passage of time, the number of responsibilities
of ASHA will itself become a challenge for her to cope up with. This will not only reflect in the
quality of her work and performance but ultimately fail in fulfilling the very objectives with which
the initiative was initially conceptualized. As the initiative is still in the early stages, the Committee
suggests that the Department should review the responsibilities entrusted to the ASHA. Committee’s
attention has been drawn by the findings of Common Review Mission which conducted appraisal
of NRHM in November, 2007, 16 months after NRHM got final Cabinet approval in July, 2006.

against activities/conflicts regarding compensation money, and lack of role clarity between ASHAs
and AWWs are two major problem areas identified. The Committee apprehends that situation may
worsen with more complexities arising in future. The Committee, therefore, is of the view that role
of ASHA needs to be reassessed and reformulated.

We agree with the observations. Accordingly, NHSRC has agreed to review the
responsibilities of ASHA, AWW and ANM.
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
The Committee notes with a sense of relief that the Department has at last come to
concur with the observations of the Committee regarding its apprehensions on the role clarity
and feasibility of discharging the duties assigned to ASHA. The Committee would like to state
here that these apprehensions were voiced by it in earlier reports so that the objective with

Department has stated in its Action Taken Note that National Health System Resource Centre
(NHSRC) is reviewing the ‘job r esponsibilities’ and “Role clarity of ASHA” as well as that of
AWW and ANM. The Committee observes that the Department has not specified any
timeframe, within which NHSRC would be completing its review. In the meantime, these
Social Health Activists would continue discharging their duties originally mandated with the
likelihood of new ones adding to their responsibilities. The NHSRC has to complete its review
in a time bound manner so that such an important health initiative does not become
redundant. The Committee, therefore, urges upon the Department to ensure the timely
submission of the Report by NHSRC, followed by expeditious implementation of the same.

those 318 MMUs sanctioned in 2006-07, was set as the target to be achieved during 2007-08 under

Recommendations/Observations
3.16.2 The Committee had the opportunity to apprise itself about the key findings of the appraisal
conducted by the Common Review Mission in November, 2007. The study is based on team visits
made to one or two districts in Andhra Pradesh., Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Orissa, M.P., Gujarat,

J&K, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Tripura, U.P. and West Bengal. The Committee finds that assessment

NATIONAL VECTOR BORNE DISEASE CONTROL  PROGRAMME
Recommendations/Observations
4.7 The Committee notes that increased supervision and monitoring is one of the main strategies
adopted for effective control of malaria. The latest figures made available to the Committee reveal
continuance of shortage of surveillance and supervisory staff in NE States. In the biggest State of
NE Region, Assam against sanctioned posts of 694 Health Supervisor (Male) only 570 were in
position, against 343 Health Supervisors (Female), there were 316 and only 1647 MPW (M) against
sanctioned posts of 3080. What is more disturbing is that while Tripura failed to furnish the data,
Meghalaya and Nagaland have provided incomplete information. The primary role of MPW (M) and
MPW (F) is door to door surveillance and detection of communicable diseases and it’s reporting.
The fact that these functionaries play a vital role in disease detection and surveillance cannot be
ignored. By not appointing these functionaries, the States leave a big gap at the field-level disease
surveillance, detection and treatment. This vital issue needs to be pursued at the highest level in
the concerned States. The other strategy adopted is use of Rapid Diagnostic Kits by ASHAs. The
Committee does not have high expectation from this initiative as firstly, required numbers of ASHAs
have to be in place in malaria endemic States and even if they are there, they would be over-
burdened with the various tasks already assigned to them. The Committee fails to comprehend the
continuance of such a discouraging situation inspite of special dispensation for NE States. The
Committee can only reiterate that there is need for drastic measures and extensive monitoring under
the supervision of State Nodal Officers.

94

Considering the workload of the ASHA, initially 61 Districts of 11 States have been identified for

JAPANESE ENCEPHALITIS
Recommendations/Observations
4.10 Japanese Encephalitis (JE) is a viral disease with a tendency of seasonal outbreaks. JE has
been reported repeatedly from 15 States out of which, Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Haryana, Karnataka,
Kerala, Maharashtra, Manipur, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal have been reporting
repeated outbreaks. There is no specific anti viral drug for JE and cases are managed
symptomatically. Efforts have been directed to provide technical support and strengthen capabilities
of States through training to tackle this disease. A vaccination programme for children between 1
and 15 years of age under the Universal Immunization Programme, using single dose live attenuated
SA-14-14-2 vaccine has been launched in 2006. In 2006, 11 districts in 4 States were covered
which was expanded to 28 districts in 10 States during 2007. A total of 93.08 lakh children were
vaccinated against the target of 105.31 lakh children achieving 88.39% coverage. As per the Annual

95
Report, 2007-08, the vaccination campaign has so far been completed in Assam (89%), Haryana
(86%), West Bengal (61 %) and in 7 districts of Uttar Pradesh (99.7%).
The Committee is dismayed to note that despite various methods adopted by the Department
over the past year, to contain the disease, the number of cases reported to be suffering from JE/
AES has shown an increase over the previous year figures. The fact is even more disturbing that
though the Department claims to have completed 99.97% immunization in the past year in 7 worst
affected districts in Uttar Pradesh, the situation there has worsened with 2675 cases and 577
deaths in 2007 (till December) over the 2006 figures of 2320 cases and 528 deaths. The Committee
fails to comprehend as to why inspite of a number of preventive measures taken by the Central
Government in co-ordination with the State Government of Uttar Pradesh, the JE/AES related cases
and deaths continue to be high in the State. The Committee apprehends that the actual figures
would increase the tally much further. The Committee would like to take the opportunity to State
that though the data for Assam has not been made available by the Department, going by the fact
sheet of 2006, it is apprehensive that the situation in Assam would also show a similar trend as
that of U.P.
Action Taken
About 88% was covered during 2007 in 27 districts. 4022 cases and 963 deaths were
reported.
Infection with JE virus may be asymptomatic or may cause febrile illness, meningitis,
myelitis or encephalitis. Encephalitis is the most commonly recognized presentation of JE and is
clinically indistinguishable from other causes of acute encephalitis syndrome (AES) which may
include meningococcal meningitis, TB meningo encephalitis, viral encephalitis, JE, Cerebrospinal
meningitis and even cerebral malaria, hence since 2006 Dte. of NVBDCP issued guidelines to report
JE under AES. The CSF/sera samples collected for AES cases are subjected to serological testing
and for the past three years, JE positivity has fallen from 39% in 2005 to 14.2% and 13% in 2006
and 2007 respectively. Though 51 Sentinel sites with manpower and equipment for serological
testing have been identified in 12 JE endemic States by Dte. NVBDCP, all the samples are not
tested due to constraints in laboratory testing. Secondly, in Eastern Uttar Pradesh, apart from JE
other viruses like enterovirus (EV76&89 strains) are circulating in the community which was
established by NIV, Pune during 2006 as out of 306 CSF and 179 sera samples, only 36% and
18% JE positivity was reported from these samples. In addition, 21.56% (EV76&89 strains) and
1.96% Coxsackie ‘B’ was detected in 6 CSF samples. It is pertinent to note that vaccination is
given against JE only.
Recommendations/Observations
4.11 The Committee would like to draw the attention of the Department to the fact that the
year 2006 had reported a visible impact of preventive measures initiated by registering a declining
trend when compared with 2005 figures. Quantum jump in the first three quarter of 2007 calls for
a serious review with special focus on Assam and U.P. the two main endemic States. The
Committee would impress upon the Department that analysis of epidemiological and entomological
data for epidemic outbreak prediction and timely remedial measures is required to be carried out
on an urgent basis.
The Committee feels that perhaps the precautionary methods adopted by the Department
have not percolated properly to the affected population because of which the disease has once
again registered an increase. The Committee adds that lax monitoring of the disease by the Central
as well as the State Governments could aggravate the situation further unless it is dealt with a
sense of urgency. It suggests the Department to undertake on-the-spot review of the situation as

96
to the possible causes for upsurge in the reported cases. The Committee urges the Department to
step up the ongoing mc activities in the endemic States so that the desired objective is reached
soon.
Action Taken
The JE situation in Eastern UP is reviewed at regular intervals by Additional DG and
Director, NICD. The last meeting was held on 12.05.08. Apart from above, Dte. of NVBDCP set
up JE sub-office and Vector Borne Disease Control unit (VBDCU) in Gorakhpur in February and
April, 2007 respectively. The main task assigned to the sub-office of VBDCU is to closely monitor
JE situation by making field visits, collecting entomological/epidemiological data, analyzing and
interpreting the same in consultation with Dte. of NVBDCP and sharing it with district authorities
for immediate remedial measures. During 2007, two multidisciplinary Central Teams were deputed
to Gorakhpur and Saharanpur districts (30.7.07 to 6.8.07) and 25-31 October respectively.
Recommendations of both these teams were discussed with concerned State/district officials for
immediate corrective measures. The States are also supported by providing funds for various JE
components. JE kits are also supplied to all JE endemic States by Dte. NVBDCP. During 2008, all
the States were sent advisories for preparing Action Plan on Prevention and Control of AES/JE on
5.02.08. It was followed by sending a check list indicating month wise activities on 25.02.08. On
19.03.08 a one day workshop was organized at BRD Medical College, Gorakhpur on
clinical manifestations and case management. Experts from NVBDCP helped the States/district
authorities to draw up a field oriented Action Plan in a meeting held under the Chairpersonship of
Principal Secretary (Health) and F.W., Government of Uttar Pradesh on 20.03.08. A central multi
disciplinary team of 6 experts also visited the State and BRD, Medical College, Gorakhpur w.e.f.
13-15 May, 2008 for making an on the spot assessment on the requirement of manpower, civil
works and equipment for establishing AES treatment unit as desired by HFM, Government of India.
Dte. NVBDCP organized 2 days workshop cum training at Lucknow on surveillance and
case management on 30-31 July, 2008 which was attended by 40 participants including 35 officials
from 11 endemic districts and 5 State officials.
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
The Committee observes that a number of measures have been initiated by the
Department in co-ordination with the State authorities with regard to control of Japanese
Encephalitis (JE) in eastern U.P., the most endemic area. The Committee also takes note
of two problem areas - one of constraints in lab-testing and prevalence of other viruses,
apart from JE with vaccination being available only against JE. The Committee fails to
understand why, inspite of adequate funds being provided under the Programme, proper
sample testing facilities have been lacking. The Committee would like to State here that
lack of proper serological testing facilities would result in improper detection of infected
cases and could aggravate the situation further. The Committee suggests that mobile labs
for conducting the required test may be introduced so as to supplement the existing
facilities and to overcome the constraints faced in lab testing. The Committee would
appreciate if such an initiative is implemented at the earliest by the Directorate of NVBDCP
after due consultation with the State and district authorities in the JE infested Areas in
Assam and U.P.
The Committee would like to point out that problem of other viruses, apart from JE
in eastern UP was deteted by NIV , Pune in 2006. By now, strategy for tackling these viruses
including vaccination should have been in place and being implemented. The Committee,
therefore, impresses upon the Department to take the required action on an urgent basis.

CHIKUNGUNYA
Recommendations/Observations
4.16 State-wise analysis of suspected Chikungunya cases and number of confirmed cases during
2006 and 2007 reveals a very disturbing trend about the spread of this disease. In 2006, maximum
number of confirmed cases were reported from Maharashtra (804) followed by Karnataka (298)
and Gujarat (225). In contrast, Kerala reported the highest number of confirmed cases of 909 while
there are 347 confirmed cases occurring in West Bengal in 2007 up till November. Another cause
of serious concern is overall increase in total number of confirmed Chikungunya cases from 2001
in 2006 to 1876 in 2007 (upto November).
Recommendations/Observations
4.17 Incidence of Chikungunya cases in the country during 2006 and 2007 has led the
Committee to the conclusion that various initiatives taken by the Department have so far failed to
yield any desired results. The Committee strongly feels that with the enhanced allocation of
Rs.14.59 crore in 2008-09 for Dengue and Chikungunya, effective measures are required to be
undertaken in the affected States. Mere circulation of detailed guidelines and advisories for
prevention and control of these diseases to all affected States would not serve any purpose. What
is required is to identify the affected districts and go for regular fever surveillance in such endemic
areas to detect an unusual trend. The Committee is of the view that if this analysis of ground
reality is followed by IEC activities and strengthening of apex Referral Institutions for diagnosis and
treatment, number of Dengue/Chikungunya cases would show a declining trend. The Committee
apprehends that unless adequate remedial measures are taken, sporadic outburst of these diseases
would continue to be reported from different States every year.
Action Taken
During 2007,59535 cases for Chikungunya were reported. Total 7850 samples tested out of
which 1826 was confirmed for Chikungunya virus.
During 2006-07, Rs.21.60 crores was released as emergency package to the affected States
for items like Fogging Machines, Pyrethrum Extract, Temephos and Insecticide-treated bed nets
and IEC activity. Subsequently in 2007-08, Rs.8.75 crores was released as emergency package to
the affected States for items like Pyrethrum Extract, Temephos and IEC activities including social
mobilization of the community.
During 2006, Chikungunya disease appeared in the country after acquiescence of almost
three decades. The community did not have immunity against this disease and 1390322 suspected
cases of Chikungunya were reported by 16 States/UTs respectively. Only 15961 samples (1.15%
of suspected cases) were tested, of which 2001 were confirmed for Chikungunya virus (12.5%
of the samples tested).
In 2007, due to the intensification of implementation of the strategic action plan for
prevention and control of Dengue and Chikungunya in the country including community based
vector control and intensification of focused IEC activities, the number of suspected cases were
only 59535 i.e. 95.72% less than 2006 from 14 States. Besides, in 2007 Government of India had
established 110 Sentinel Surveillance hospitals in the affected States for proactive surveillance and
diagnosis. In addition, 13 Apex Referral Laboratories were also identified and linked with these 110
Sentinel Surveillance Hospitals for providing advanced diagnostic facility and back up support.
Therefore, due to better facility in 2007 more samples could be tested and confirmed, total 7850
samples tested (13.2% of suspected cases) and 1826 confirmed for Chikungunya virus (23.3% of
the samples tested).

98
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Department in intensifying multi
pronged approaches to contain the incidence of Dengue and Chikungunya cases. The
Committee feels that results of such measures would surely reflect in the numbers of cases
detected for the year 2008. The Committee would like to be apprised about the IEC
interventions undertaken in this regard.
Committee’s attention is, however, drawn to the number of samples tested against
the suspected cases. The Committee notes that out of 59,535 suspected cases in 2007 only
13.2% were tested and of these 13.2% cases (7,850 samples tested), 23.3% of the samples
turned out to be confirmed cases. The Committee feels that 13.2% samples tested is a
fairly low number compared to the suspected cases figures and given the fact that more
than 23% turned out to be confirmed cases of the 7,850 tested samples, the figures could
be much more if the number of samples tested were increased.
The Committee apprehends that in such a situation, there are chances of there being
a large number of confirmed yet undetected cases. The Committee, therefore, suggests that
the Department should concentrate its efforts towards strengthening the testing lab
facilities so that maximum number of samples are tested.
V. NATIONAL T.B. CONTROL PROGRAMME
Recommendations/Observations
5.7 The Department has informed the Committee that over 2400 NGOs, 17,000 Private
practitioners, and 120 corporate houses have been involved in the provision of RNTCP services in
the Programme during 2007-08 under various components of the Programme. The Committee, in
its earlier report, had suggested that a forum can be evolved where participating NGOs/PPs get the
opportunity to share their experiences with similar workers from other States. At the same time,
the Committee would also recommend that the evaluation of the work being done by NGOs/PPs
be made under the Routine Programme Evaluations carried out by the States (2 districts per
quarter) and the Centre (2 districts per month) in order to review the progress made under the
mc initiatives and suggest proper utilisation of the funds allocated under the scheme. In reply to
the above recommendation, the Department had stated that in all the Central Evaluations conducted
in two districts per quarter, a representative from CTD goes to review the PPM activities both at
the district and State level. Similarly, the State evaluations also carry out the PPM review with
respect to utilization of funds and activities undertaken by the NGOs.
The Committee would like the Department to furnish details of the evaluation reports as
stated above with respect to utilization of funds and activities undertaken by the NGOs. The
Committee would also like to suggest here some measures for increasing advocacy, communication
and social mobilization. It recommends that the Department should sit with the Private Print and
Media sector and should work out modalities as to how they can be involved in the IEC activities
for the programme.
Action Taken
Under the Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP), involvement of NGOs has
been decentralized to the District level and MOUs are signed with the District TB Societies. Funds
to NGOs are released by the concerned District TB Society in accordance with the terms and
conditions of the MOUs. Many NGOs also participate without any financial assistance. Evaluation
of performance of NGOs/PPs is an integral part of Routine Programme Evaluations carried out by
the States and the Centre. Few examples of different schemes being implemented by the NGOs in

99
the districts and reviewed during internal evaluation of the districts are placed at Annexure-VI. In
addition, an independent evaluation of selected NGOs will be conducted and the report is likely to
be available by the third quarter of current year.
There was a Consultation on NGO/PP guidelines on 29-31st Jananuary, 2008 wherein 60-
70 NGO/Private practitioners were invited from all over the country to share their experiences in
Public private partnership in RNTCP implementation. The successful models as well as constraints
