XVII NATIONAL TOBACCO CONTROL PROGRAMME (NTCP) 
 
17.1 The National Programme on Tobacco Cont rol (NTCP) aims to help implement the 
provisions of ‘Cigarettes and other Tobacco Products (Prohibition of Advertisement and 
Regulation of Trade and Commerce, Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 2003’ and 
also to bring about greater awareness, sen sitize about the harmful effects of tobacco 
consumption and provide tobacco cessation facilities.   
  
17.2 The Committee is constrained to observe that in 2007-08 and 2009-10 BE funds 
had to be revised downwards substantially at the RE stage keeping in view the pace of 
expenditure under the Programme. Against an  allocation of Rs. 40.00 crore and 30.00 
crore in 2007-08 and 2009-10 respectively, an expenditure of only Rs. 13.98 crore and Rs. 
16.60 crore has been reported.The Committee opines that time and again the 
Department brings the rhetoric of scarcity of funds and here it is not utilizing the 
available resources persistently. The Commi ttee may be informed of the measures 
taken by the Department to optimally utilize the available resources under this 
Programme.  
 
17.3 The Committee observes that launched as  a pilot project in 12 districts of 6 
States in 2007-08, by the end of 2009-10, Programme has been extended to only 42 
districts of 21 States.  It would not be wrong to conclude that the Programme continues 
to be run on a pilot basis even after three year  of its launch.  This is the position when 
the target was to extend the coverage to 100 districts by the end of 2008-09. 
 
17.4 Committee’s attention has also been drawn by the progress made w.r.t. the setting 
up of the National Tobacco Regulatory Author ity. Proposed to be set up in 2008-09, the 
present position is that its setting up is unde r consideration of the Ministry. Further, as 
regards Referral Labs for testing of Tar and Nicotine contents in various tobacco 
products, the Committee has been informed that the Government has approved the 
setting up of tobacco testing labs under th e National Tobacco Control Programme. The 
Ministry will soon issue tenders for procur ement of equipment for the proposed tobacco 
testing labs. 

 64
 
17.5 The Committee would like to remind th e Department that subsequent to its 
examination of Demands for Grants of  the Ministry for 2008-09, in its 27 th Report, it 
had taken a strong view of the fact that despite the ‘in principle’ approval of the 
Planning Commission for setting up of the National Regulatory Authority and 
Referral Labs for testing Tar and Nicotine content and initiation of the process for 
seeking approval of the competent authority, no progress had been made for quite 
some time.  Accordingly, the Committee had called for concerted efforts of the 
Department to achieve the approval of th e competent authority for setting up of the 
National Regulatory Authority. However,  as per information available with the 
Committee now, there has been ‘no’ improvem ent on this front even after a period of 
two years. The Committee is dismayed at the Department’s attitude in this regard.  
National Tobacco regulatory Authority is supposed to be pivotal to the whole 
Programme to help in effective implementation of Tobacco free initiatives. Even the 
progress w.r.t. setting up of tobacco testing labs has not seen any improvement. To 
aggravate the matter further, the Depart ment has not been able to expand the 
Programme in more districts of the country as scheduled. Even the first Adult Tobacco 
Survey has been lingering on for quite some time. The Committee is upset with the 
way things are being managed under the Programme. Fixing realistic targets on paper 
is only the first step towards achieving a goal and the Committee does find the targets 
set to be realistic and achievable. Therefore,  it is not able to comprehend itself with 
the reasons for the delay in achieving the targets. The Committee would, therefore, 
recommend some urgent and concrete action plan in achieving the targets set under 
the Programme in a time bound manner.  
 
17.6 In response to a query in respect of the Department’s efforts to generate mass 
media/ IEC campaign regarding harmful effe cts of tobacco products, the Committee is 
given to understand that Rs 14.91 crore wa s released during 2009-10 for advertising and 
publicity activities.  The Committee also notes that an enhanced amount to the tune of Rs. 
23 crore has been earmarked for 2010-11 for this purpose.  
 

 65
17.7 The Committee is happy to note that the Department is focusing on Mass 
Media/ IEC campaign to generate awareness among the common people about the 
harmful effects of tobacco products. Awareness among the common masses, especially 
the younger generation, is the key to success of the whole Programme. The Committee 
would recommend that events like coming Commonwealth Games, venues of cricket 
and other matches being played in India, public gathering like the kumbh melas etc. 
may also be utilized to generate awareness among people with Mass Media/ IEC 
campaign at the sites. 
 
17.8 The Committee notes that the State Go vernment /UTs are the main enforcing 
agencies for implementing provisions of th e Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products 
(Prohibition of Advertisement and Regula tion of Trade and Commerce, Production, 
Supply and Distribution) Act (COTPA), 2003. However, litigation in Supreme Court and 
High Courts against various provisions of COTPA and Rules made thereunder have been 
cited as a major barrier in effective implementa tion of the Act. To tackle such issues,  a 
Steering Committee has been constituted for taking suo-moto action with regard to 
violation of the Act. State Governments have also been advised to form State/Districts 
level Steering Committees. Inter-Ministerial ta sk force has been constituted to sensitize 
stakeholders on cross cutting issues of tobacco control and implementation of COTPA. 
Department has also stated that strengthen ing of legal support and establishment of a 
dedicated Tobacco Cell in the Ministry and co nstitution of National Tobacco Regulatory 
Authority will help in effective implementation of Tobacco free initiatives.  
 
17.9      The Committee notes that though  the Department has been able to come up 
with a law for restricting use and sale of the Tobacco products, the ground realities 
have not changed much. The various provisions of the Act are not being implemented 
in letter and spirit even in metro cities in India. Situation in respect of small towns 
and rural areas can well be imagined. The Department cannot remain a silent spectator 
on such vital issues. A proper pro-active st rategy should be developed whereby all the 
States are roped in to work sincerely in this regard.

XVIII            MEDICAL EDUCATION 
18.1 The Committee is given to understand that at present, there are 300 medical 
colleges in the country. Out of this, 229 ar e recognized medical colleges and 71 medical 
colleges which have been approved for runn ing MBBS courses will be considered for 
recognition as per the provisions of Medica l Council of India (MCI) regulations. The 
Committee is informed that while there is no provision for review of MBBS courses every 
five year, MCI carries out periodic inspection  of medical colleges as per the provision of 
IMC Act, 1956 and Regulations made there-un der to maintain the standards of medical 
education in the country. The medical co lleges which are found not meeting the 
requirement as per the regulations are given an  opportunity to rectify the deficiencies. In 
the recent past, MCI has recommended for with drawal of recognition in respect of 10 
medical colleges. Besides, MCI has also issued show cause notices to 15 medical colleges 
and sought compliance report. On receiv ing the compliance report from college 
authorities, MCI will verify the same  and, wherever necessary, submit its 
report/recommendations to the Central Go vernment for appropriate action. For the 
academic year 2010-11, recommendations from MCI are awaited in respect of 59 medical 
colleges for grant of annual renewal of perm ission for which the last date is 15.5.2010. It 
has also been informed that so far, 4 medica l colleges have filed court cases with regard 
to withdrawal of recognition.   
 
18.2 The Committee is concerned with the fact  that as many as 10 colleges are being 
considered for withdrawal of recognition and 15 more being issued show cause 
notices. From the large number of colleges caught compromising the standards while 
being scrutinized, it is clear that all is not well. This clubbed with the fact that these 
colleges are those which have come under scheduled scrutiny and there may be many 
which keep on functioning until they come under inspection scrutiny, makes the 
matter more serious.  The Committee would lik e to have a brief about the status of 
inspection of all the medical colleges inter-alia containing – the selection procedure 
vide which the colleges are selected for inspection, the date of establishment of 
college, date of inspection/s, shortcomings noticed and action taken during the last 5 
years. The Committee may also be informed of the details w.r.t. the progress made for 

 67
withdrawal of recognition of 10 colleges, show cause notice to 15 colleges and the court 
cases in respect of the 4 colleges.  
 
18.3 The Committee is given to understand th at as per Section 11(2) of the Indian 
Medical council Act, it is for the college authorities to apply for recognition to the Central 
Government through the relevant University  when the first batch of MBBS students 
appears for final year examination. Medical Co uncil of India carries out the inspection of 
the Applicant College and recommends to the Central Government to accord recognition 
to the medical degree if all facilities are av ailable at the medical college as per MCI 
norms. In respect of a pointed query regardin g the latest status with respect of medical 
colleges seeking recognition vis-à-vis their final batch of students appearing in the 
examination, the Committee has been informed that there are 15 medical colleges where 
the first batches of MBBS students have appe ared for final examination but are yet to be 
recognized in the academic year 2010. The recommendations in respect of these medical 
colleges are awaited from Medical Council of India.  
 
18.4 The Committee is not inclined to agree with the Department’s view that all is 
well with the existing procedure for reco gnition of MBBS degree colleges. The 
Department cannot escape from its responsibility by citing that it is the responsibility 
of the individual colleges to seek re cognition. The Committee opines that the 
Department needs to have into consideration the psychological impact of such a 
situation on the final year students who in its opinion would be more anxious to see 
their college getting recognit ion rather than taking their examinations seriously. The 
Committee is of the considered view that the whole procedure of recognition should 
be complete well before the final year  students take their examinations. The 
Committee therefore recommends to the Depa rtment to revisit its stand on the issue 
and come up with some concrete steps. A status note on the issue of recognition to 15 
medical colleges where the first batches of MBBS students have appeared for final 
examination in the academic year 2010 may be furnished.  
 
18.5 The Committee observes that out of 20,880 Bachelor of Dental Surgery seats, 1990 
remained vacant in 2007-08; 4347 out of 22,500 remained vacant in 2008-09 and 1651 out 

 68
of 23,570 remained vacant in 2009-10. The Committee also takes note of the fact that there 
are only 11,000 jobs created nationally in the Government Sector with  no projection of 
increase. However, the Dentists are eligible to practice privately and teach in private 
dental colleges. But the Committee is also aware of the limitations of the private sector to 
consume this supply.   
 
18.6 The Committee also notes that in 2004,  Dental Council of India proposed a 
moratorium on new colleges and addition of  new seats in existin g institutions for a 
minimum period of 5 years which was not ag reed to by the Government. The Committee 
is also informed that recently, the DCI has sent a proposal to the Government to make 
norms of opening new college more stringen t which includes replacing the 100 bedded 
hospitals in dental institution with an a ffiliation to an approved/recognised medical 
college in the interest of clinical traini ng and quality education, which is under 
consideration. Further, the Council has proposed to restrict the attachment of 
Government General Hospital with one dental college only irrespective of beds available 
there which is also under con sideration. Stringent criteria  for infrastructure and the 
requirements of publications for faculty have  been enforced. A central bio-metric system 
to monitor the presence of faculty on the day to day basis has also been introduced.  
 
18.7 The Committee is in full agreement with the initiatives proposed by the DCI 
especially in view of the fact that so many seats are lying vacant year after year. 
Further, the Committee is of the firm opinion that education and accordingly the 
number of seats should be need based an d keeping in view the demand and supply 
scenario. Here, by the figures available with the Committee, it is amply clear that there 
is an urgent need for intervention to bala nce the same. In view of the above, the 
Committee recommends to the Department to take some urgent steps in consultation 
with the DCI and the various State Governments, so that this unwanted trend is 
arrested at the earliest and precious resource s are utilized purposefully in other areas 
of medical education. The Committee also recommends to the Department to actively 
consider the proposals submitted to it by the DCI regarding making norms of opening 
new college more stringent.

generic medicines while India is still followin g branded medication pattern. India is the 
only country where generic branded and branded medicines are sold in the open markets.

generic branded medicines with manifold pric e tag in comparison to generic medicines.  
The Committee also notices that even if there is no difference of formulations, therapeutic 
use and the quality between a generic and branded machine, yet the branded and generic 
branded medicines are being sold at substantiall y higher prices in the open market.  Thus, 
the poor and the common men are forced to shell out extra money when they approach the 
chemist to buy such medicines which in the opinion of the Committee needs to be 
addressed with the sense of urgency.  The Co mmittee is further given to understand that 

 74

financial debts.  Besides, procurement of  the branded/generic branded medicines for 
Govt. hospitals, dispensaries and CGHS leads to heavy burden on the Exchequer 
comprising of precious taxp ayer’s money.  The Committee, therefore, recommends the 
Department to make it mandatory for the Go vt. hospitals and CGHS to procure only 
generic medicines so that their procuremen t cost is reduced substantially without 
compromising on the quality and efficacy of such medicines.  The Committee further 
recommends the Department to initiate some measures so that generic medicines are not 
marketed and sold as generic branded medicines leading to exorbitant prices by the 
profiteering companies so that such medici nes are available to the common man at 
reasonable prices.  The Committee also recommends that it should be made mandatory 
for the Government Doctors to prescribe on ly generic medicines. The Committee may 
be informed of the action taken by the Department in this regard.

expenditure was made.  Again, in 2009-10 an initial outlay of Rs. 100 crore were 
made under the same head which was revised upwards to Rs. 150 crore and no 
expenditure is reported to be there up till January, 2010. Approved outlay of Rs. 
1500 crore for the Eleventh Plan has thus remained unspent in spite of three years 
of the Plan period being over. 
 
2.5 The Committee strongly feel that poor planning and execution on the part of 
the Department regarding the various on-going schemes have been responsible for 
such a discouraging scenario. The Committee is well aware of the fact that in a vast 
country like ours, with healthcare facilities specially in the rural areas showing a 
negligible presence, need for additional fu nd will also be there.  The Committee has 
also been strongly advocating the case fo r enhanced allocation of funds for NRHM 
but the trend of under-utilization/ unutilis ation weakens the justification for higher 
provision of funds. The Committee is also aware of the fact that Union Government 
alone cannot achieve the targeted goals. It has to carry out the implementation with 
the active support of State Governments. The Committee, therefore, once again 
recommends the Department to make its monitoring mechanism more effective so 
that such large amount of funds do not lapse/remain unutilized. The Committee also 

 78
suggests the Department to undertake a comprehensive self-assessment study on the 
means and methods used to improve financ ial accountability under the Mission so 
far, and based on the findings, to devise  a mechanism whereby funds utilization for 
the rest of the Mission period could be in a better state. Taking note of significant 
and persistent shortfall in utilization of the budgeted funds, the Committee would 
like the Department to exercise greater prudence in their budget formulation and 
make their estimates only after proper assessment and planning. 
 
 2.6 NRHM is targeted to provide accessible, affordable and equitable health care 
services for people living in rural areas of the country with focus on under-served 
population and marginalized groups. Therefore, it is the considered view of the 
Committee that              under-funding should not be allowed to come in the way of 
delivery of essential and quality health care  to the most vulnerable sections of our 
society. The Committee, therefore, recommen ds that additional funds be allocated 
under NRHM wherever required. 
 
2.7 The twin problems of pending Utilizati on Certificate (UCs) and Unspent Balances 
under various programmes/ components of NRHM have been engaging the attention of 
the Committee since long. The Committee finds that the year 2009-10 was also no 
different. The Committee was informed that as on 1
st April, 2009, there were 2083 UCs 
amounting to Rs. 7785.90 crore outstanding in respect of grants released upto March, 
2008. This pendency must have increased manifold by the end of March, 2010.  
 
2.8  On being asked specifically about the measures taken by the Department to 
liquidate pending Utilization Certificates, the Department has informed that as per the  
provision of the General Financial Rules it is necessary that in case of recurring grants, 
funds for the same purpose beyond 75% of the next year’s provision will not be released 
unless audited Utilisation Certificate for the grants released in the previous year is 
received. Further, for non-recurring grants, no fresh releases are being authorized unless 
audited Utilisation Certificate for grants released in the year prior to the last year (i.e., 
with a ‘grace period’ of one year) has been received.  
 
2.9 Besides that, this matter, apart from being regularly monitored in the Department, 
is also annually reviewed with the State Financial Advisers by Secretary (Expenditure) 
and the Union Finance Minister separately. And as a further effort to maximize 

 79
liquidation of UCs, a DO at the level of Secretary (Health) has been issued to all the 
Principal Health Secretaries of the States co ncerned. Lastly, with the intent to improve 
financial accountability, Financial Monito ring Groups comprising of MBAs, CAs, 
Accounts & Finance Managers are being deployed at the State-level under NRHM. 
 
2.10 The Committee observes that 2083 num ber of pending UCs amounting to Rs. 
7785.00 crore is too large to be comfortable with. The Committee notes that the 
biggest defaulters in terms of amount involved in pending UCs are Uttar Pradesh 
(Rs. 1097.39 crore), Karnataka  (Rs. 596.08 crore), Bihar (Rs. 537.74 crore) and 
Assam (437.11 crore) and unreconciled amount is to the tune of Rs. 707.40 crore 
involved in 31 UCs. The Committee is also astonished to find that the pendency of 
UCs has been continuing year after year, esp ecially in case of the High Focus States,  
EAG States and NE Region, although well ov er two-thirds of the time period of 
NRHM( 2005- 2010) is over. What is more astonishing is that  Union Territories like 
Delhi, Chandigarh, Puduchery and A&N Islands also figure in the list.  
 
2.11 The Committee would like to point out that mere advisories/ DOs to States 
for liquidation of pending UCs is not a tenable solution for expeditious liquidation 
of pending UCs. The Committee is of the view that monitoring of pending UCs 
needs to be further strengthened. The Committee also recommends that a senior 
officer be assigned the task of laising wi th the States and monitor the progress in 
this regard on a quarterly basis. The Co mmittee would like to be apprised of the 
action taken to revamp the monitoring of pending UCs. The Committee is also of the 
view that the Department take up the matter with the States showing maximum 
pendency of UCs at the highest level impressing upon them the imperative of 
furnishing the UCs timely and exercising fiscal discipline.

III INFRASTUCTURE STRENGTHENING 
 
Healthcare Units  
 
3.1 NRHM aims at strengthening of Primary Health Infrastructure and improving 
effective service delivery across the country. Sub-centers, Primary Healthcare Centers 
and Community Health Centres are the three cornerstones on which rural infrastructure is 
built upon. The Secretary, during the course of deposition before the Committee on 6 th 
April, 2010, highlighted the overall progress ma de in the achievement level of different 
healthcare infrastructure of NRHM, stating that as on date 1,46,036 Health Sub Centers  
(HSCs) were functional with 9144 new HS Cs taken up for construction and 8997 for 
renovation; 23,458 PHCs were functional with 8324 PHCs  functioning 24X7 while 1009 
new PHCs have been taken up for construction and 2081 for renovation. Out of 4276 

 82
CHCs– 930 were added after NRHM. Among the District Hospitals (DHs), 578 District 
Hospitals were functional with 57 new DHs  being constructed and 357 DHs have been 
taken up for renovation. Besides, 2463 centres were functioning as First Referral Units.  
 
3.2 The Committee while taking note of progress made in strengthening the 
primary health infrastructure after the la unch of NRHM would like to point out 
that considerable gap still continues to pe rsist. In this connection, Committee’s 
attention has been drawn by Performance Audit of NRHM by CAG (Report No. 8 
of 2009-10) there was a shortfall of 43987 Sub-Centres (27%) in 22 States/ UTs, 8613 
PHCs (31%) in 21 States/ UTs and 4200 CHCs (55%) in 23 States./ UTs which were 
required to be created during the NRHM period (2005-12). Target of creation of 
30% of new infrastructure by 2007, i.e. 13196 sub-centres, 2585 PHCs and 1261 
CHCs could not be fulfilled. According to the CAG Report, as many as 14 States/ 
UTs failed to take any initiative for bridging the gap. Out of the target of 43987 sub-
centres 8613 PHCs and 4200 CHCs only 2562 Sub-centres, 685 PHCs and 138 CHCs 
could be set-up. The Committee only hopes that 935 Sub-Centres, 178 PHCs and 67 
CHCs reported to be under construction during CAG Audit must have been 
completed and become fully functional by  now. The Committee would like to point 
out that even as per the target of 2007, there was a shortfall of 9749 sub-centres, also 
1722 PHCs and 1056 CHCs. Against this backdrop, bridging the gap of 43987 sub-
centres, 8613 PHCs and 4200 CHCs by the end of mission period i.e. 2012 seems to 
be an uphill task. The Committee would like to be point out that the targets set up 
under NRHM were as per the population norms of 2001. The shortfall of 
infrastructure is bound to increase manifold once 2011 census is over and 
population norms revise. The Committee has also taken note of the fact that only 
very few states like Assam, Chhatisgarh,  Rajasthan, Uttarkhand and Lakshadweep 
had made an attempt to achieve the target of 2007, while the remaining states 
reported nil achievement. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Department has to pursue vigorously with all the non-performing states, otherwise 
even the basic objective of NRHM of havi ng the minimum required infrastructure 
would also remain unfulfilled.  
 
3.3 On a query about the progress in the construction work of sub-centres under the 
‘Infrastructure Strengthening Project’of NRHM, the Committee was informed that the 

 83
progress of Sub-Centre construction is being followed on priority basis to ensure 
functional facilities at Sub-Centre level across the country at the earliest. As per RHS-
2008, out of total 1,46,036 Sub-Centres functioning across the country, a total of 78,803 
were functioning in Government buildings, and  9684 SCs were being constructed across 
the country. The Committee was given to under stand that estimated cost of construction 
is Rs.968.4 crores at the rate of Rs.10 lakhs for 9684 sub-centres, for which funds were 
released through NRHM Flexible Pool.  
3.4 The Committee is perturbed to find that out of 1,46,036 Sub-Centres, as many as 
67233 Centre are functioning from rented bu ildings. From the details furnished by 
the Department, the Committee finds that a large number of States have simply 
failed to take benefit from Central funds being provided for construction/ 
upgradation of sub-centre buildings. In St ates/UTs like Himachal Pradesh, J&K, 
Tamil Nadu, A&N Islands, D&N Haveli, Daman & Diu, Chandigarh, Lakshadweep, 
Puducherry no construction activity has been  initated so far. In States which have 
taken some initiative in this regard, per centage of sub-centres being strengthened/ 
upgraded is very low.  
3.5 The Committee is not convinced by the clarification given by the Department 
that in some States, sub-cen tres are working in other Go vernment buildings/ spaces 
provided by Panchayats etc. The Committee also apprehends that condition of PHC 
and CHC buildings would also be no better. The fact remains that there is an urgent 
need for undertaking a review of present condition of all the Sub-centre/ PHC/ CHC 
buildings across the country and undertak e the required construction under a time-
bound Action Plan.  
 
3.6 The Committee’s attention is also drawn by the damaging report given by 
the CAG in its latest report on this cr ucial aspect. As per CAG report, among

4.15 ASHA - a social health activist - is one of the most important strategic

Role of ASHA 
 
4.22 The Committee notes that the major job responsibilities  of ASHA are :- 
-           awareness generation on  Health, RCH, HIV/AIDS among the people. 
-           advising newly married couples for their special needs. 
-        providing escort services to and guiding pregnant women for availing of 
institutional facilities for Anti-  Natal, Natal and Post-Natal needs. 
-          counselling on nutrition, pregnancy, breast-feeding, immunization and 
family planning 
-          stablishing link with PHCs, private providers and others for service 
requirement of beneficiaries. 
-           mobilising parents for child survival interventions 
-           promoting basic sanitization 

 99
-           provision of non-clinical spacing contraceptives 
-           surveillance of communicable diseases. 
 
4.23 Apart from all these, ASHA is also the primary interface conferred with the duty

V. RCH FLEXIBLE POOL 
 
5.1 The main objective of RCH Flexible Pool is to bring about the change in the three 
critical health indicators: Infant Mortality Rate (IMR), Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) 
and Total Fertility Rate (TFR) consistent with the goal of National Population Policy 
2002, the Tenth and Eleventh Plans and Millennium Development Goals (MDGs). The 
targets to be achieved by the year 2012 are to  bring down IMR to less than 30, MMR to 
less than 100 and TFR to 2.1. Against this, the achievement levels as per latest available 
studies are: IMR 53 (SRS 2008), MMR 254 (SRS 2004-06) & TFR 2.6 (SRS 2008). One 
of the most important strategies adopted under the Programme is the freedom given to the 

 103
States to prepare their Annual State and District level Project Implementation Plan (PIPs) 
after assessing their need- based requirements.  
 
5.2 Secretary, Health, during her presentation before the Committee, highlighted the 
main strategies for Maternal Health and stat ed that the main factors for high rate of 
MMR could be broadly classified as delay in decision-making, delay in reaching the 
hospital and delay in initiating appropriate care. Delay in decision-making takes place 
mainly due to lack of awareness and financ ial constraints. The Committee was informed 
that to tackle these basic constraints, a nu mber of significant interventions have been 
made so far. Awareness and counseling through ASHAs/ ANMs/ AWWs, availability of 
financial assistance through Janani Suraksha Yojana for institutional delivery, and skilled 
providers for domiciliary birth were cited as the main interventions. The other problem 
area coming in the way of checking MMR was delay in reaching the hospital due to lack 
of knowledge about danger signs and availability of transport facilities. Here again, 
ASHAs/ ANMs/ AWWs are meant to do the counseling on danger signs.  Transport 
facilities are being made available through JSY and referral services through 
Government ambulances/ PPP arrangements. Another hindrance noticed was lack of 
availability of operational facility for tracking pregnancy and its complications. The 
Committee was given to understand that these hindrances were being tackled by 
upgradation of infrastructure at the district level and multi-skilling of Doctors to 
overcome shortage of critical specialists. As  on date, 1024 doctors have been trained in 
anesthesia skills, 543 doctors trained in obstetric skills and 37,162 Staff nurses/ LHVs/ 
ANMs trained as skilled birth attendants.  
 
5.3 The Committee was also apprised about the main factors found responsible for 
high rate of IMR, which were severe infec tions (36% deaths), pre-term birth (25% 
deaths), birth asphyxia (23% deaths) and neo- natal tetanus (4% deaths). Steps taken so 
far for checking this high incidence of neo-na tal deaths were Integrated Management of 
New Born and Childhood Illness, Basic New Born Care and Navjat Shishu Suraksha 
Karyakaran etc.

6.1 The National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme is a comprehensive 
programme for prevention and control of vector  borne diseases namely Malaria, Filaria, 
Kala-azar, Japanese Encephalitis (JE), Deng ue and Chikununya which is covered under 
the overall umbrella of NRHM. Central Gove rnment provides technical and financial 
assistance and also logistics support and the State Governments have to meet the other 

 114
requirements and operational costs. NE States are provided 100 per cent central 
assistance under the programme.  
6.2 The general strategy for prevention an d control of vector borne diseases under 
NVBDCP is through Disease Management,  Integrated Vector Management  and 
Supportive Interventions.  The Committee was informed that for the year 2010-2011, 
the Directorate of NVBDCP has projected their demands amounting to Rs.698 crore. 
However, allocation of Rs.418 crore has been  made considering overall allocation of 
Ministry of Health & Family Welfare. Out of the allocation of Rs. 418.00 crore for 2010-
11, the EAP component is Rs 165.26 crore (GFATM 84.87 crore and World Bank 80.39 
crore).  
6.3 The Committee notes that against an allocation of Rs. 442.00 crore in 2009-
10, expenditure reported as on 28.02. 2010 was only Rs. 278.61 crore. The 
Committee observes that this trend of under-utilisation of allocated fund is also 
there in the first two years of the Eleventh  Plan. Against the provision of Rs. 399.50 
crore and Rs. 472.25 crore in 2007-08 a nd 2008-09, expenditure was only Rs. 383.66 
crore and Rs.  299.38 crore respectively. Th e Committee is constrained to observe 
that against the total Plan outlay of Rs. 3190.00 crore for the Eleventh Plan, less 
than half of the funds were released and that too remained under-utilised. 
Committee’s repeated attempts for optimum utilization of allocated funds under 
NVBDCP has failed to make any impact. 
6.4 The Committee has always been responsive to the genuine demands of the 
Department. The Committee would, however, also like the Department to focus on 
better utilization of the scarce resource s. The Committee, once again, recommends 
that the Department need to focus on analyzing the reasons for reduced utilization 
of the allocated funds and take corrective action accordingly.  
 
The Committee would also like to know whether any commitment charges 
are to be paid by the Department in case of shortfall in utilization of EAP 
component and if so, the charges paid during the last three years.

Committee, therefore, recommends that th e Department should, in coordination 
with the State Government concerned, chal k out an action plan to achieve the 
targeted coverage of JE vaccination and also apprise the Committee of the progress 
made in this regard. Similar efforts for vacc ine coverage of the affected districts of 
Andhra Pradesh, Assam and Tamil Nadu are also required.   
6.19 The Committee would also like to be apprised of the progress made towards 
establishing sentinel sites for regular surveillance and Apex Referral Laboratories 
for advanced diagnosis, circulation of stan dard guidelines, capacity building and 
intensive IEC campaign and vaccination with single dose under Universal 
Immunization Programme. Keeping in view th e fact that Uttar Pradesh is the most 
endemic State which contributes 80% of JE cases, the Committee recommends that 
the Government must quickly take a decision on conducting a special JE 
vaccination campaign for left out children in the seven most sensitive districts of 
Uttar Pradesh along with the affected di stricts of Andhra Pradesh, Assam and 
Tamil Nadu. The quarterly progress made in this regard may be communicated to 
the Committee. 
6.20 The Committee was also informed that apart from establishing field unit of NIV, 
Pune at BRD Medical College, Gorakhpur for de tecting and isolating non-JE viruses, the

guidelines have already been circulated to all the affected districts in the State for 

 120
initiating control measures against entero-vir uses. The diagnostic facilities have been 
strengthened at 50 sentinel and 13 Apex Refe rral Laboratories including 15 sentinel sites 
established in Uttar Pradesh. These have been supplied with diagnostic kits free of cost

VII NATIONAL TB CONTROL PROGRAMME  
 
7.1 Tuberculosis is a major public health problem in India. The country accounts for 
nearly one-fifth of the global incidence. In 2007, out of the global annual incidence of 
9.23 million TB cases, 1.96 million were estimated to have occurred in India, of whom 
0.8 million were infectious cases. About tw o persons die from TB in India every three 
minutes; 900 people every day and almost 3.28 lakh every year. The Committee was 
informed that the Revised National TB C ontrol Programme (RNTCP) has been extended 
to the entire country in 2006. Till date, 11 million T.B. patients have been initiated on 
treatment with 2 million additional lives saved. 
  
 7.2 To tackle HIV/TB co-infection, TB + HIV collaborative activities with 
NACP, initiated in 2001, have been scaled up across the country. The Committee 
notes that intensified TB/HIV package of services have been started in nine HIV 
high prevalence States (Andhra Pradesh, Goa, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Manipur, 
Mizoram, Nagaland, Pondicherry and Tamil Nadu) in 2008 and has been extended 
to nine additional States (Delhi, Gujarat, Punjab, Rajasthan, Kerala, Assam, West 
Bengal, Orissa and Chandigarh) in 2009-10 with a vision to cover the entire nation 
by 2012. Monitoring of co-infected patients was started from 4
th quarter of 2008, 

 121
and out of a total of 31047 such cases, 5171 cases were treated with a 75 per cent 
success rate. The Committee is happy to note that the Department has been pursuing its 
concerns diligently to identify and provide treatment to HIV/T.B co-infected patients. 
  
7.3 To control this major health problem of the country, Revised National TB Control 
Programme (RNTCP) based on internationa lly recommended strategy of Directly 
Observed Treatment Short Course (DOTS) . The Programme has the objective of 
detecting at least 70% of cases and curing at  least 85% of sputum positive patients. In 
order to address the problem of Multi Drug Resistance TB (MDR-TB), establishment of a 
network of 43 accredited Culture and Drug  Susceptibility Testing Laboratories for 
diagnosis and follow-up of MDR TB patients across the country was being undertaken in 
a phased manner. It is planned to roll out se rvices for Drug Resistant Tuberculosis in all 
State/ UTs by March 2011. 
7.4 The Committee observes that the emergence of multi-drug resistant TB has 
increased the severity and magnitude of the problem in terms of cost, longer and 
difficult treatment regimen. In this contex t, the Committee welc omes the initiative 
of establishing a network of 43 Laboratories for diagnosis and follow-up of MDRTB 
patients. The Committee hopes that such Laboratories will be set up across the 
country in such a way that people from all parts of the country have equity in access 
to such facilities. The Committee would like to have an idea of the location of such 
Laboratories and also of the structure of charges, if any, proposed to levied for 
availing of the facilities therefrom.

8.1 The goal of leprosy elimination at the Na tional level is less than 1 case per 10000 
population. National level elimination of Leprosy has been achieved since 31
st December,

prevalence of leprosy started late, due to late introduction of Multi Drug Therapy (MDT) 
for treatment of leprosy.  D & N Haveli being an industrial area has large number of 
migratory cases from nearby States/UTs, and du e to less population, a small increase in 
the number of recorded cases resulted in enormous increase in the prevalence rate.

of ASHAs, focused attention in endemic blocks, urban areas, training of all General 
Health Services functionaries for leprosy diagnosis and management and Intensified 
Information, Education & Communication (IEC).

III CENTRAL GOVERNMENT HEALTH SCHEME (CGHS) 
 
The Committee is unhappy to note the continuous underutilization of Plan 
funds during the first three financial years of the Eleventh  Plan, more so when the 
Department had sought an increase of funds during the RE stage during 2008-09 and 
2009-10 and it could not even utilize the funds provided to it at the BE stage. The 
Committee, therefore, strongly feels that the Department has to justify the need for 
additional funds by ensuring optimum utilization thereof and be careful in 
placing/proposing its revised estimate so that funds are not unnecessarily blocked and 
go unspent.                                                                                                                        (Para 3.3) 
The Committee does not find any logic for under provisioning for CGHS under 
Materials & Supplies as also for IT activ ities Head which are bound to affect the 
quality of services available to the CGHS beneficiaries. The Committee also observes 
that total tentative pendency with regard to medical claims of pensioners as on 
January, 2010 is Rs. 200 crore, including bill s pertaining to 2008-09.  In such a scenario, 
allocation of Rs. 377.87 crore for pensioners  against the projected requirement of Rs. 
627.00 crore for 2010-11 is bound to increase th e pendency further.  The Committee is 
of the view that full allocation of required funds has to be there so that pensioners are 
not made to face uncalled for hardships.                                                                    (Para 3.5) 
 The Committee is happy to note that a number of initiatives under CGHS are 
proposed to be undertaken during 2010-11. On e such initiative is expansion of a pilot 
project for Preventive Health Check-up for pensioners and serving employees over the 
age of 40 years at CGHS dispensary, Sect or-12 and Sector-4, R.K. Puram, New Delhi . 
The Committee would like the Department to share its experiences of the pilot project 
and recommends to the Department to expand the initiative to more dispensaries in a 
time-bound manner.                                                      (Para 3.6) 
 The Committee also welcomes the introd uction of a proposal under which the 
empanelled hospitals will forward the bill for the treatment of pensioner CGHS 
beneficiaries to UTI-TSL and payment of the same within 10 days.  Such an initiative 
is bound to help the pensioners in availing of healthcare without any hindrance.  
                       (Para 3.7) 

 140
The Committee views the introduction of the current proposal of the Ministry 
with serious concern. The Committee is no t convinced by Department’s categorical 
statement that it does not intend to replace the CGHS with this new insurance scheme. 
It is amply clear that the scheme would be mandatory for future employees and 
pensioners.  The Committee would like to point out that CGHS is one of the very 
important social security measures which ha s been providing health care services at 
economical rates to its beneficiaries for so many decades. The Committee fails to 
comprehend the rationale for depriving all the beneficiaries of such an essential 
service in the long run.  The Committee would like to point out that there is a well-
structured set up of CGHS dispensaries, Govt. Hospitals providing allopathic and 
AYUSH healthcare and also a number of empanelled diagnostic centres and private 
hospitals.  In the recent years a number of initiatives have also been taken for 
strengthening/revamping different comp onents under the Scheme.  A number of 
additional dispensaries are also proposed to be set up in the near future.  The existing 
CGHS scheme is part of the social responsibility of Govt. for its serving/retired 
employees. Full reimbursement as per th e prescribed norms is payable to the 
beneficiaries. There is no upper limit on annual expenditure on the treatment of a 
beneficiary.  The very idea of capping the amount of coverage to Rs. 5 lakh per family 
per year as well as the limit of coverage to only - Self, spouse, two dependent children 
and dependent parents and thereby forcing for payment of the fixed percentage of 
premium per additional dependent family member under the proposed scheme 
indicates that the Govt. intends to dilute its social obligation primarily to its 
employees. This is unacceptable to the Committee.                         (Para 3.9) 
The Committee is dismayed at the Departme nt’s approach from the very outset.  
First, it had taken the plea of a large number of private hospitals and diagnostic centres 
empanelled under the CGHS and the opposition  from the staff side to any such move. 
Then, subsequent to Committee’s recommendation that flexible timings are order of 
the day and  desirable in the interest of many of the CGHS beneficiaries who are 
unable to avail the facilities of dispensaries in the morning hours, the Department in 
its Action Taken Note on Committee’s 27
th Report had stated that the Ministry intends 
to take the matter before the Committee of Secretaries. The latest reply proves beyond 
doubt that the Department is not willing to move forward in the matter. Like in the 

 141
previous instances, the new plea taken by the Department is its inability to go ahead 
on account of its existing staff strength.  The Committee is of the opinion that if there 
is shortage of manpower, necessary action plan may be drawn up and approval sought 
for requisite manpower at appropriate level. The Committee would like to reiterate 
that the matter needs to be taken up seriou sly and in the right spirit.  The Committee 
would like to be informed of the progress made in this regard.         (Para 3.11) 
 
 The process of computerization under the CGHS which was initiated during 
2005 is continuing. The Committee notes that finally the Department has been able to 
finish the work of computerization in six cities i.e. Delhi, Kolkata, Nagpur, Pune, 
Chennai and Ranchi and it is nearing comp letion in Hyderabad, Mumbai and Patna. 
However, the Committee is constrained to no te that the Department has not been able 
to add momentum to the computerization wo rk even after the expiry of about five 
years as 15 cities still remain to be covere d. The Committee therefore recommends that 
the computerization work in the remaining cities be completed in a mission mode by 
the end of the Eleventh Plan.              (Para 3.12) 
 
 The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Department to neutralize the 
teething problems afflicting the smooth implementation of the computerization. 
However, the ground realities are not much encouraging. The Committee is informed 
that there is shortage of computer operat ors and the doctors have to first see the 
patients and then feed the relevant data in the computer system leading to delays and 
the resultant long queues. This way the computerization has only been able to help 
keep a check on the inventory in the store room and save time in putting up request 
for local purchases wherever required. Howe ver, it has not been able to obviate the 
problems faced by the beneficiaries particularly the old age pensioners who have to 
stand for long hours in queue. The Committee,  therefore, recommends that adequate 
trained manpower may be made available at the earliest.                     (Para 3.14) 
 
3.16 The Committee is happy to note that after much delay the Department has 
finally been able to open a dispensary each in NOIDA and Dwarka. However, as the 
number of CGHS beneficiaries is very la rge in that area, the Committee recommends 

 142
to the Department to put all its acts togeth er to start the three dispensaries for which 
plots have been purchased in Dwarka and one dispensary at Gurgaon. 
                  (Para 3.16) 
 The Committee is given to understand that the workload on the dispensaries in 
Delhi has increased manifold. The Committee therefore recommends to the Department 
to have a realistic assessment of workload in CGHS dispensaries in Delhi with a view 
to explore opening up of new dispensaries to mitigate the problems faced by the 
beneficiaries. The Committee would recomm end to the Department to furnish a 
detailed status note on the no. of beneficiaries attached with each dispensary, zone-
wise in Delhi and the NCR and plans of the Department to open new dispensaries in 
underserved areas of Delhi and NCR. The Committee may also be briefed about the 
availability of unused land lying with CGHS in different cities covered by CGHS 
alongwith the purpose of their acquirement.            (Para 3.17) 
 
 The Committee is not very happy with the element of adhocism in such a 
crucial area. The Committee would like to point out that the number of vacancies in a 
particular grade are bound to put pressure on the existing workforce thereby 
compromising with the quality of services provided to the beneficiaries. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends to the Department to urgently chalk out a strategy 
to fill up the vacant positions in all grades under CGHS in a time-bound manner.  
                  (Para 3.21) 
 
 The Committee has noticed substantial variation in approved rates of 
investigations / treatment procedures in various metro cities. The Committee does not 
find much merit in the argument of the Department that rates offered by the private 
hospitals and diagnostic centres depend upon the prevailing market rates, number and 
business volume from CGHS beneficiarie s likely to be derived by eligible 
institutions/private institutions, which vary from city to city. The Committee is of the 
opinion that substantial variation of 50 to 100 per cent in approved rates and that too in 
cities like Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolk ata cannot be considered commensurate 
with the variation in economic dynamics. The Committee accordingly, recommends to 

 143
the Department to come up with a strategy to  counter this variation of rates by having 
minimum disparities in the rates.                        (Para 3.23) 
  
 Though the Committee appreciates Department’s initiative for ensuring quality 
service to CGHS beneficiaries and has no doubts over the professionalism of 
NABH/NABL, yet it does not find much merit in making it compulsory as a 
precondition for empanelment under C GHS. The NABL/NABH lay down certain 
norms and standards to be observed and on inspection, they provide accreditation to 
those who fulfill the said standards. There is no guarantee that once accredited, the 
Hospital/diagnostic centre will maintain those standards till the next inspection by 
NABL/NABH. Further, it has been observed that many of the reputed hospitals don’t 
go for accreditation under them. In such a scenario it may be counterproductive as the 
beneficiaries may be deprived of services  under such reputed Hospitals/diagnostic 
centres. The Committee accordingly recommends to the Department to be cautious on 
this move.                             (Para 3.25) 
 
 The Committee would also like to have  information regarding the number of 
NABH/NABL accredited Govt. hospitals/diagnostic centres as well as private 
hospitals/diagnostic centres empanelled under CGHS.                     (Para 3.26) 
 
 The Committee would like to point out that prior to 2001, all the premier 
specialized Hospitals had opted for CGHS empanelment.  The Committee wonders as 
to whether the recently empanelled Hospital of Delhi can provide the same services as 
being provided by Rajiv Gandhi Cancer Ho spital or Dharamshila Cancer Hospital.  
The Committee is also not aware about the quality status of the only empanelled 
Hospital.  The Committee reiterates that the kind of specialized services being offered 
by a particular hospital, specially for terminal diseases like cancer and not the lowest 
rates should be the basic criteria for selection of a hospital.  One must not forget that 
the main objective of CGHS is to provide qu ality health care at economical rates. Not 
only this, Government is supposed to reimbu rse only the packages rates.  Payment of 
difference in treatment expenditure is the co ncern of the beneficiary.  In Committee’s 
view, package rates need to be governed by quality service.  Nobody stops the 

 144
concerned authorities to negotiate with the applicant hospitals for arriving at mutually 
acceptable package rates. It cannot be that services offered by a small hospital can be 
considered on an equal footing with an advanced well established hospital.  The 
Committee, accordingly, recommends framing of a policy for revision of rates after 
every two years to realistically fix the ra tes of treatment. The Committee may be 
informed about the action taken by the Department in this regard.        (Para 3.28) 
 
 The Committee appreciates the number of initiatives taken by the Department 
for effective functioning of CGHS. The Committee however, feels that wide publicity 
through local and print media needs to be given in this regard.  Only then CGHS 
beneficiaries will be in a position to avail of such facilities.                     (Para 3.30)
   
IV SAFDARJUNG HOSPITAL AND VARDHMAN MAHAVEER MEDICAL 
COLLEGE, NEW DELHI 
 
 The Committee notes that against projected Plan requirement of Rs. 180.60 crore

fact that out of the RE plan allocation of Rs. 129.92 crore for 2009-10, the Hospital was

th February, 2010, with every possibility of full

 The Committee is very concerned with the vacancy position in different 
categories of posts at the Hospital. This coupled with the admission of the head of the 
Hospital itself that the sanctioned strength is far below the practical requirement, 
presents a sorry state of affairs. The Co mmittee is of the opinion that vacancies 
irrespective of any category are not only directly or indirectly bound to have an 
adverse impact on the quantity and quality of the services rendered by the Hospital 
but also result in overstressing of the existing staff. Further, the vacancies also have 
the potential to affect the quality of education imparted at the attached medical 

 145
college. The Committee is given to understand that in case of Resident Doctors, 
vacancies occur frequently and are filled regularly depending on the requirement. The 
Committee is, however, not able to comprehend as to why there is about 25% of

action so that it has the next batch of Reside nt Doctors available to  step-in in place of 
the outgoing Resident Doctors. Similarly, vacancies in Group A and Group B Gazetted 
posts are far above the justifiable limits.  The Committee accordingly recommends to 
the Department to take up the issue of vacancies seriously and on priority basis. It also 
recommends a review of the requirement of manpower vis-à-vis the sanctioned 
strength of the Hospital and college. The Committee would like to be informed about 
the progress made in this regard.                         (Para 4.4) 
 Committee’s attention was also drawn towa rds acute shortage of  nursing staff at 
the Hospital. Non-availability of good accommodation for nursing staff was cited as the 
main factor responsible for such  a situation.  Existing staff qu arters at Srinivaspuri were 
considered to be too inadequate.  The Comm ittee was given to understand that another 
project was coming up at Dwarka. The Committee is of the view that provision of

employees, especially for the nurses rendering 24 hour services.  The Committee,

nurses should be taken up on priority basis.  Viability of such facility at the Hospital 
premises itself under the ongoing Redevelopm ent Plan of the Hospital needs to be

th Report 
had urged the Department to make wholeh earted efforts to expedite the procedural

stated a timeline of six years for the entire work to complete. Keeping in view the

recommends to the Department to make all conceivable efforts so that the whole 
redevelopment work is completed within this period of six years. For this to happen,

 146
agencies need to be made accountable to  accomplish the set targets from the very

 The Committee is constrained to observe that the allocated funds for 2009-10

initiated by the Hospital do not get hampered due to scarcity of funds.           (Para 5.4) 
 
 The Committee welcomes the proposal to start a general maternity ward, 
construction of a New Casualty Building, multi-storey super speciality block and 

 147
setting up of Centre of Excellence for Mental Health. However, the Committee

VI ALL INDIA INSTITUTE OF MEDICAL SCIENCES (AIIMS) 
  
The Committee is anguished to note that out of a total allocation of Rs. 1461 
crore for the Eleventh Plan, the Institute do es not seem to be able to utilize the 
earmarked funds for the Plan period during the first three years of the Plan period. 

 148
The Institute has been able to utilize on ly Rs. 648.00 crore (as on 28-2-2010).  The 
Committee sees little hope for optimum utiliz ation of remaining funds during the last 
two years of Eleventh Plan. As a result, the initiatives/ongoing projects are not likely 
to be executed as targeted originally. Th e Committee observes that as many as 21 
projects were envisaged to be completed dur ing the Eleventh Plan for which an outlay 
of Rs. 623.63 crore was made. The Committee is, however, dismayed to note that by the 
end of the first three years of the Plan, utilization reported is only Rs. 70.18 crore. The 
situation is worsened by the fact that work in respect of as many as 14 projects is yet to 
start. These projects include expansio n of OPD Block and New Emergency Ward,

rd January, 2009.

understands that a number of projects in different areas are being handled by HSCC at

XI COMMON RECOMMENDATIONS REGARDING HOSPITALS 
 
  The Committee is concerned with the procedural hassles coming in the way of 
the developmental work in various hospitals and institutions of repute under the 
Department. Though the Committee considers the laid down procedures as means of 
systemic checks and balances, yet it finds no merit in their coming in the way of 
urgent developmental work, and that too for a project targeted at taking care of the 
health care needs of the common man of the country. The Committee is of the 
considered opinion that the imperatives of development and environmental concerns 
need to be reconciled without further loss of time to avoid further time overruns in 
respect of this project.  The Committee th erefore recommends to the Department to 
have a centralized cell under a dedicated senior officer to coordinate all such 
procedural issues with the various agencies. The Department needs to play a proactive 
role here. If required, the matter may be taken up at the senior most level to facilitate 
early sanction of requisite statutory cl earances and the concerned approving 
authorities may also be apprised of the Co mmittee’s concern over approval delays in 
this regard.  The Committee may be informed about the progress made in this regard. 
                            (Para 11.1) 
  The Committee is pained by the fact that the healthcare fraternity under the 
Department has to function under very stressful conditions.  Taking strong view of the 
enormous patient load in almost all the institutions/hospitals under the Department, 
which is in many cases manifold than envisaged, the Committee would like to make a 
general recommendation to the Departme nt.  It recommends strongly to the 
Department to have an independent reas sessment of manpower done in all the 
institutions/hospitals under it – sanctioned vis-à-vis the patient load of the hospital. 
The Committee also recommends a close mo nitoring of the vacancies in all the 
institutions/hospitals of the Department under a dedicated senior officer for 
coordination between the institutions/hospitals and the recruitment agencies so as to 
facilitate early filling up of vacant posts.                       (Para 11.2)

XIII PRADHAN MANTRI SWASTHYA SURAKSHA YOJNA (PMSSY)  
  
 Such a slow progress of implementation is bound to result in huge amount 
remaining unutilized at the end of the Plan period. The Committee had time and again

corrective measures, but it appears that the sa me has not yielded fruits atleast as of

 After an assessment of the progress of  various components under the Scheme,

th Report had made its apprehensions very clear that with the

whole lot of issues including manpower.  The Committee would like to point out that

th July, 2003.  Even after a lapse of more than six years,

 Position with regard to upgradation of 13 medical colleges is also quite

Department needs to have into consideration the psychological impact of such a

PHCs (31%) in 21 States/ UTs and 4200 CHCs (55%) in 23 States./ UTs which were

30% of new infrastructure by 2007, i.e. 13196 sub-centres, 2585 PHCs and 1261

under NRHM were as per the population norms of 2001. The shortfall of

very few states like Assam, Chhatisgarh,  Rajasthan, Uttarkhand and Lakshadweep

The Committee is also quite disappointed with the progress made over the

up the issue of non-filling up of the vaca ncies with the States/UTs. However, there

functionaries are also pivotal in the collec tion and dissemination of health related 
information from the field levels. The Comm ittee would, therefore, appreciate if 
updated data is got collected by the Department in coordination with the States/

ROUTINE IMMUNIZATION 
 
 The Committee is constrained to observe that this is yet another case of inept 
handling of budgeted funds by the Department. The Committee finds to its dismay 
that despite the efficacy and relevance of  Pentavalent Vaccine being in question, a 
substantive amount of Rs. 205.30 crore was allocated for the same out of which Rs. 
184.14 crore remained unutilised and had to be surrendered. The Committee would 
like the Department to exercise greater ca ution in future and not allow repeat of 
such fiscal imprudence.        (Para 5.13) 
  
From a perusal of the information made available, the Committee would like 
to state here that significant progress un der the Immunisation Programme has not 
been noticed in many of the States. This fa ct holds true both for the high focus and 
EAG States and also the non-high focus States .  In some instances like that of Tamil 
Nadu and Dadra & Nagar Haveli, the immu nization coverage has infact dropped 
below the DLHS II rate. The Committee observes that a low coverage rate in some 
of the very densely populated States like Bihar and Uttar Pradesh means that a very 
large number of children remain exposed to the vagaries of diseases resulting in 
high incidence of IMR in the country. The Committee observes that unless proper 
execution of the plans are made by the programme authorities, visible impact on the 

 191
immunization coverage would remain a distant dream. It, therefore, urges the 
Department to take up the issue with th e respective State Mission Directors during 
the next Common Review Mission, who need to be impressed upon to achieve the 
required quarterly/ annual targets.                                                                 (Para 5.16)                                  
 
Cold chain maintenance is the most  crucial component for effective 
implementation of the Immunisation  Programme. The Committee, however, 
observes that so far this has proved to be the weakest link under the programme. 
Committee’s apprehensions have been confirmed by the assessment of cold chain 
maintenance arrangement made under the Performance Audit of CAG. As per the 
CAG Audit, none of the cold chain equipment was available in any of the 124 test 
checked PHCs in Haryana, Meghalaya, Madhya Pradesh, Puducherry and West 
Bengal. Besides, in Bihar, Lakshadweep and Uttar Pradesh, 31 to 68 per cent of cold 
chain equipment was found non-functional.                                                 (Para 5.17) 
 
 The Committee is more disturbed by the fact that Government of India 
budgetary support for maintenance of cold chain equipments, supply of spare parts, 
provision of alternate power supply has prove d to be of no avail. The States have 
simply confirmed their inability to abso rb the funds for envisaged purposes. The 
Committee is of the view that the absence of cold chain management has indirectly 
resulted in adverse impact on the UIP, a high priority area under the Mission.                                             
(Para 5.18)

pressing forward with various measures to contain the spread of WPV-1 and WPV-

JANANI SURAKSHA YOJANA 
The Committee views with serious concern the high level of pregnant women 
registered for institutional delivery not op ting for the same. This clearly indicates 
that various interventions made under JS Y so as to make aware the targeted 
population about the positive impact of institutional delivery both on the mother 
and child have not proved to be very effective. Situation becomes more worrisome 
by the fact that high focus States where need was the most have been showing such a 
trend. The Committee fails to understand the reasons behind ground level 
functionaries not monitoring the trimeste r check-up of the registered pregnant 
women. The Committee would like to point out that the achievement of 47 per cent 
of institutional deliveries (DLHS-III 2007- 08) from 37 percent (DLHS-I  1998-99)
