VI.  RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT 
Recommendations/Observations  
6.6 Committee’s attention has been drawn by some re ports about successful treatment of Cancer patients by Ayurvedic drugs. 
On a specific query about the veracity of these rep orts, the Committee was pleasantly surprised to not e the significant 
achievements made by the Ayurvedic practitioners as indicated below:- 
- On the recommendation of the Scientific Advisory Committee (Ayurveda), the CCRAS has initiated the s tudy of 
‘CARCTOL’ a proprietary medicine of Vaid Nand Lal Tiwari of Jaipur supposed to have anti-cancer properties. For 
verifying the therapeutic claim, standardization work has been completed by the Council. Safety and toxicity studies 
have also been completed. As informed by the Ex. Director-General, CCRAS, ‘CARCTOL’ has also been subjected 
to in-vitro study at Advanced Cancer Research Centr e of TATA, Mumbai against 14 types of human cancer cells 
out of which it was found effective against pancrea tic and lung cancer. It was placed on record that C ARCTOL is 
being used for treatment of cancer: patients both i n the country and abroad. After preparation of doss iers, multi-
centric clinical trials will be conducted. 
-  Pre-clinical study of ‘Cancer Gaza Kesari’ a pro prietary drug of Vaid Krishan Gopal of Ajmer has al so been 
conducted by the Council in collaboration with Vete rinary College, Chennai. The study revealed that th e drug 
significantly reduced the mammary tumor incidence, latency, frequency, rate of growth and malignancy. It was also 
subjected to in-vitro study against 14 types of hum an cancer cell line, out of which it has shown to b e of effect 
against Pancreatic and Lung Cancer. 
-  Pilot project was sanctioned by the Ministry in 1996 to study the effects of metal based formulatio ns prepared by 
Vaid Balendu Prakash of Dehradun in the treatment of Acute pro-myllolic Leukemia. The Committee was informed 
that the drug was patented jointly by the Council w ith Germany. The Committee was also given to unders tand the 
Vaid Balendu Prakash has been treating Cancer patie nts with the drug. On a specific qucry it was clari fied that the 
Indo-German patent was a process patent. So far onl y a pilot study of 21 patients has been conducted b y the 
Council. Multi- Cultural Clinical Trials of the drug were to be undertaken which would take four years. 
-  The Committee also notes that ethical approval a nd release of funds for clinical trial of AYUSH QOL-2C at AIIMS 
has been completed. Registration of patent is to be initiated shortly. Simultaneously, 10 patients have been enrolled 
for study at St. Johns Medical College, Bangalore. This drug is reported to improve quality of life of those receiving 
chemotherapy /radiotherapy. 
Action Taken  
 The encouraging observations of the august committ ee have been noted.  

Recommendations/Observations  
6.7 The Committee places on record its appreciation  of commendable work being done by the Research Cou ncils on their 
own and also in collaboration with well-known institutions in the country and abroad. Work of the CCRAS touches both routine 
ailments as well as chronic ailments where permanen t cure is yet to be found inspite of giant strides made by the modern 
medical sciences. In such a scenario, for the treat ment of the most deadly cancer disease, any signifi cant achievement by any 
system of medicine should be welcome to all. The ‘C ommittee considers it a strange irony that although  large number of 
patients are getting relief by the drugs formulated by individuals after years of their single-handed research, official recognition 
still remains elusive to them. The Committee strong ly advocates the streamlining and expediting of the  official certification 
process, so that humanity at large gets the long-awaited relief. 
Action Taken  
 Whenever any claim is submitted to Council, the sa me are examined and put before Scientific Advisory Committee to 
carry out scientific validation. In this context, t wo claims on cancer have been subjected to Pre-clin ical Studies based on which 
clinical trial will be carried out as per lead. If any drug is finally marketed, the benefit will be s hared by Council and the 
claimant. But there is no provision of Certification by the Council. 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE  
 The Committee is not satisfied with the evasive re ply given by the Department. Keeping in view that t here is no 
effective cure/treatment for cancer in the modern s ystem of medicines, the Department should make all out efforts to 
exploit any significant achievement by any system o f medicine towards treatment/cure of such a deadly disease. The 
adequate and effective mechanism should be in place  to expedite scientific validation of any claim in this regard. The 
Committee notes with dismay that the Department has  failed so far in carrying out-scientific validatio n of such claims 
due to procedural delays and lack of adequate resea rch work and expertise in this regard. The Committe e would 
reiterate once again that the process of clinical t rial on two claims of cancer needs to start at the earliest. Contention of 
the Department that in the event of any drug being finally marketed, the benefit would be shared by the Council and the 
claimant, does not lead to the ultimate goal of pro viding relief to patients suffering from cancer. It  is a well-known fact 
that this disease is spreading at an alarming rate with new dimensions emerging. In such a scenario, t he Department 
along with the Research Council needs to play a pro-active role.

IX.  QUALITY CONTROL OF AYUSH DRUGS 
Recommendations/Observations  
9.1 The AYUSH system of medicine is governed by Dru gs & Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules made thereunder. Enforcement 
provision of Chapter IV A of Drugs & Cosmetics Act,  1940 is the responsibility of State Governments. E stablishment of State 
Drug Testing Laboratories is also a statutory responsibility of States under the Act. To provide financial assistance to States for 
strengthening enforcement mechanism, the Drug Quali ty Control Scheme was started in IXth plan. Over th e years, 29 State 
Drug Testing Laboratories and 46 State Pharmacies h ave been set up and upgraded @ Rs.1.50 crore/DTI, a nd Rs. 2.00 
crore/pharmacy. In the Eleventh plan the scheme was  revised to include three new components of strengt hening of the State 
enforcement mechanism, upgrading the in-house testi ng facilities of manufacturing units and assisting manufacturing units 
desirous of obtaining higher GMP like EU and WHO-GMP. 
9.2  The Committee notes that inspite of major chan ges in the scheme, fund utilization status has been  far from satisfactory. 
Against an Eleventh Plan outlay of Rs.225 crore, fu nds amounting to only Rs. 45.00 crore could be allo cated during the first 
three years of the plan period and expenditure reported upto 15th March, 2010 is only Rs.26.52 crore. 

9.3  The Committee finds that out of 29 Drug Testin g Laboratories assisted financially so far, 17 labs  are established in terms 
of equipment and buildings. Other labs are in diffe rent stages of construction of building and procure ment of equipment. Only 
46 ASU&H pharmacies have been covered under the Scheme so far. 
9.4 Committee’s attention has also been drawn by th e very low number of GMP compliant ASU&H Drug manuf acturing 
units in the country. Out of total 9837 such units,  only 4663 units are GMP complying units. Ratio of GMP compliant /non-
GMP compliant units is very unsatisfactory with the  maximum gap noticed in States like Assam, Haryana,  Kerala, Madhya 
Pradesh, Maharashtra, U.P., Tamil Nadu, Uttarakhand , Punjab. As many as 2336 legal notices have been i ssued/licenses 
cancelled so far. 
9.5 The Committee has taken note of a number of cor rective measures suggested during the Mid-term Appr aisal of Eleventh 
plan. The Committee would like to emphasize that qu ality control and quality assurance are the major i ssues with reference to 
ASU drugs. The Committee, therefore, recommends tha t corrective measures as suggested in the Mid-term Appraisal may be 
initiated without delay. 
Action Taken  
 Mid term appraisal was done for the Centrally Spon sored Scheme for Quality Control of ASU&H drugs for  the effective 
implementation of the scheme. A meeting was held on  15.10.09 in the Planning Commission. Under the sch eme Rs. 2.30 erore 
has been spent till now. Other corrective measures are being taken for effective implementation. 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE  
 This is yet another instance of casual reply by th e Department. Instead of furnishing a comprehensive  reply 
detailing the specific measures being taken/contemplated to be taken towards overcoming the shortcomings as identified 
in the mid-term appraisal, the Department has merely made a generic statement which, in the opinion of the Committee, 
is tantamount to being evasive. The Committee, acco rdingly, recommends to the Department to shed more light on the 
measures being taken for addressing the shortcoming s, especially those concerning quality control and quality 
assurance. 
Recommendations/Observations  
9.6 The Committee also takes note of the fact that the rules regarding proper labeling on Ayurvedic, S iddha, Unani and 
Homoeopathic (ASU & H) drugs are not being complied  with strictly. The Committee feels that the absenc e of proper labeling 
on ASU & H drugs may be a cause of health hazards. The Committee therefore, recommends that the monitoring mechanism in 
this regard be streamlined to ensure proper labeling on ASU & H drugs.  
Action Taken  
 Chapters IV A of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 and Rules 1945 have been enforced. The responsibili ty of State 
Drug Licensing Authorities of ASU&H drugs to implem ent all the sections and rules of this Act. Secreta ry, Department of 
AYUSH is also reviewing the status position for the  implementation and enforcement of the Chapters IV A or the Drugs and 
Cosmetics Act 1940 and Rules 1945 with the State Drug Licensing Authorities or ASU&H drugs from time to time. Instructions 
have also been issued for stick compliance of labeling provision on ASU&H drugs by the State Licensing Authorities. 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE  
 The Committee is well aware that compliance of labe ling provision on AYUSH drugs as mandated under the  
Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules made thereu nder is the responsibility of State Drug Licensing Authorities. 
Merely writing to the State Governments in this reg ard from time to time will not ensure the complianc e of this very 
crucial condition. The Committee has been repeatedl y emphasizing the need for having an effective moni toring 
mechanism for quality control of AYUSH drugs both w ith the objective of protecting the consumers’ inte rest as well as 
propagation of this alternative system of medicine.

its disposal. The Committee would also like to be a pprised of the specific measures taken by the Department to sensitize 
the State Governments and existing institutions to come forward with proposals for funding under PPP and the outcome 
thereof. The Committee also recommends that all the  stakeholders should be kept informed about vast po tential of 
AYUSH medicines available in the country.   (Para 2.1.5)  
Strengthening of Pharmacopoeial Laboratories 
 The Committee observes that the savings under the above head occurred in 2007-08, 2008-09 and 2009-10  due to 
non-filling up of posts, delay in supply of instrum ents by HSCC (India) Ltd., delay in construction wo rk and non-
finalization of recruitment rules etc. The Committe e is constrained to observe that these problems wer e not of 
insurmountable nature and could have been easily so rted out had the Department pursued the matter vigo rously with 
the agencies concerned. If it takes almost three ye ars for the Department to finalize recruitment rule s for the posts and 
get necessary approvals from local authorities, it is a sad commentary on its functioning and calls in to question its 
seriousness of exercising fiscal prudence. Now that all the groundwork has been completed, the Committee would expect 
the Department to monitor the progress in respect o f all items of work meticulously and come up with s ubstantive 
achievements in this regard.   (Para 2.1.6)  
Setting up of National Board for Medicinal Plants 
 The Committee would like to state that the Nationa l Medicinal Plants Board (NMPB) has the primary mandate of 
coordinating all matters relating to medicinal plan ts and support policies and programmes for growth o f trade, export, 
conservation and cultivation of medicinal plants. D espite the above fact, only Rs. 40.00 crore could b e made available 
out of a provision of Rs. 50.00 crore made in BE 20 09-10. Taking note of the fact that the expenditure  under this head 
was Rs. 39.19 crore as on 15th March, 2010, the Com mittee is pretty certain that the entire allocation  under this head 
must have been utilized by the end of the financial  year 2009-10. The Committee observes that while th ere have been 
recurrent savings under some of the heads with the budgeted amount being surrended year after year, su ch an 
important initiative as setting up of NMPB had to suffer financial cruch due to skewed priorities of the Department. The 
Committee would, therefore, tend to infer that ther e was something wrong with prioritizing policy of D epartment of 
AYUSH and impress upon it to be more careful in this regard.   (Para 2.1.6)  
CGHS Ayurveda Hospital and Educational Institutions 
 The Committee feels pained to note that despite ti mely placement of funds at the disposal of CPWD, it  could not 
utilize the same. The Committee would like the Depa rtment to ascertain the reasons for the same from C PWD and 
apprise it about it. The Committee feels that this delay is an issue of governance and our fast-growin g country cannot 
afford to continue with slow-moving mindset of yest erday. The Committee would also like the Department  to address 
the issue of non-filling up of vacant posts with a renewed vigor and apprise it of the progress made in this regard. 
        (Para 2.1.6)  
Pending Utilization Certificates 
 The Committee regrets to note that despite the Dep artment’s claim of persistently pursuing the matter  with the 
concerned State authorities and of its efforts proving efficacious in liquidating the UCs, the amount involved in pending 

Utilization Certificates is still substantial. For example, out of Rs. 107.61 crore released upto 2005-06, UCs amounting to 
Rs. 93.00 crore are still pending. Similarly, the a mount involved in pending UCs in the States mention ed in the table 
above is too high to be comfortable with. The Commi ttee feels that the liquidation of UCs is not being  pursued as a 
priority, but has been reduced to a ritualistic exe rcise where routine meetings are held and letters e xchanged. The 
Committee is of the opinion that monitoring of liqu idation of pending UCs needs to be done by a dedica ted officer of 
senior rank who should focus more on innovative measures and outcomes rather than routine follow-up measures.  
      (Paras 2.2.2 & 2.2.3)  
 The Committee is happy to note that in pursuance o f its recommendation, the Department has identified  the 
contributory factors for the allocated funds lying unaccounted for. From a perusal of the reasons enum erated by the 
Department, the Committee finds that solutions to t he problems highlighted are all in the administrati ve domain of the 
State Governments and if sincere initiatives are taken, they can be taken care of, facilitating more efficient use of scarce 
resources. The Committee notes that the key remedy suggested in the four regional meetings with 21 State Governments 
in this regard is to establish separate Directorate  of AYUSH and also keep separate Budget head in the  State for 
implementation and better utilization of funds earm arked for AYUSH. The Committee desires to be appris ed of the 
success achieved in this direction.   (Para 2.2.4) 
Utilization of Plan Allocation for North Eastern States During the Eleventh Plan 
 The Committee is happy to note that in pursuance o f its recommendation regarding chalking out a speci fic action 
plan for optimum and judicious utilization of alloc ated funds in N.E. Region, a Resource Centre has be en set up at 
Guwahati and a pilot project for establishment of 5 0 bedded/l0 bedded hospitals in N.E. States has bee n launched. 
However, the Committee feels that enabling an objec tive assessment of the initiatives taken by the Dep artment is an 
imminent necessity for evaluating the success of the initiatives and formulating adequate response to various drawbacks 
noticed in the process. The Committee, accordingly,  recommends to the Department to carry out an asses sment of the 
measures/initiatives taken by it to increase the absorptive capacity of the N.E. States.   (Para 2.3.2)  
III.  STATUTORY INSTITUTIONS 
 Almost four and a half years have elapsed since th e Committee presented its Report on the Indian Medi cine and 
Homoeopathy Pharmacy Council Bill, 2005 to Parliame nt on 28th July 2006. The Committee feels that the Pharmacy 
Council should have become a reality long back. Now that a revised draft has been prepared for seeking approval of the 
Cabinet, the Committee is sanguine that the Departm ent would take positive measures in this direction.  However, the 
latest feedback from the Department clearly indicates that a proposal mooted by it for setting up a National Commission 
for Human Resources in AYUSH Systems would also hav e under its jurisdiction the proposed Pharmacy Coun cil. The 
Committee is rather disappointed by this developmen t. Keeping in view the prolonged procedure involved  for 
completing all the formalities for setting up a sta tutory body, the Committee can only ‘conclude that in the near future, 
there is little hope for having either the Indian M edicine and Homoeopathy Pharmacy Council or the Nat ional 
Commission for Human Resource in AYUSH Systems. The Committee, therefore, would appreciate if the issue is finally 
decided and the required statutory body is in place at the earliest.   (Paras 3.2 & 3.3)  
 The Committee is happy to note that a number of in itiatives have been undertaken by the Department fo r 
updation of Central Registers of Indian Medicine an d Homoeopathy. Such corrective measures were long o verdue. The 
Committee would like to emphasize that by the end of Eleventh Plan, both the Registers should be fully updated.  
       (Para 3.7 & 3.8)  
IV.  HOSPITALS AND DISPENSARIES 
Expansion of Ayush System Under CGHS 
 The Committee notes that the Department is not abl e to meet the targets set in 10th Plan of providing  financial 
assistance to CGHS for opening 7 Ayurvedic, 7 Homoe opathic, 3 Unani and 2 Siddha dispensaries alongwit h 2 Yoga 
units. The Department has not bothered to comment o n meeting the target set for 11th Five Year Plan. T he Committee 
would like to be apprised of the current status in this regard.   (Para 4.3.2)  

 It is very strange that though the Mid-term assess ment of Eleventh Plan had emphasised to provide AYU SH 
facilities in 10 CGHS dispensaries by 2011-12, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has decided t o halt any 
further expansion of infrastructure in CGHS on the ground that a Health Insurance Scheme is being cont emplated for 
Central Government Employees. At a time when the avowed objective of the Government is to bridge the gaps in health 
infrastructure and human resources, the Committee i s at a loss to understand as to why such a retrogra de decision has 
been taken, especially in view of the dismal picture of health infrastructure in the country. The Committee is of the view 
that even if the CGHS is restructured, Health infra structure created under it would not go waste, but contribute to 
outreach of health care services in one way or the other. The Committee, therefore, recommends that th e Ministry 
should shed its indecisiveness in the matter and ta ke concrete action towards extending AYUSH faciliti es in CGHS 
dispensaries as per the Mid-term Appraisal of the Eltwenth Plan.   (Para 4.3.3)  
V.  EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS 
National Institute of Homoeopathy (NIH), Kolkata 
 The Committee expresses its serious concern on the  slow pace of progress in the completion of expansi on project 
for the National Institute of Homoeopathy, Kolkata.  Although it has been more than four years since th e work was 
awarded to CPWD in Mach, 2006, the Department is no t in a position to indicate adherence to the target ed date of 
completion of the project; i.e.  June, 2011. This is the state of affairs when cons tant efforts have been made to ensure 
close coordination between the Civil and Electric Division of the CPWD.   (Para 5.2.3)  
National Institute of Unani Medicine Bangalore 
 The Committee, while making the above recommendati on, had expected the Department to take expeditious action 
for creation of necessary posts for starting new Po st Graduate Courses. More than eight months have el apsed since the 
Committee made the recommendation but creation of p osts seems to have got mired in red-tape, which is evident from 
the fact that no further progress has been made during the period of last eight months. Creation of posts still remains at 
the proposal stage, pending with the Ministry of Fi nance. The Committee also takes exception to the fa ct that despite it 
recommending to the Department umpteenth number of times in the past to formulate replies in specific terms, the 
Department has chosen to merely state that “efforts  are being made to ensure creation of posts” withou t making any 
mention of the specific steps taken or proposed for  the purpose. The Committee, therefore, recommends to the 
Department to deal with the issue under reference with a sense of urgency and take tangible initiatives towards this end. 
The Committee would like to be apprised of the outcome in the matter in definite terms.   (Para 5.3.3)  
Morarji Desai National Institute of Yoga (MDNIY) 
 The Committee notes that establishing of Yoga Ther apy Centres (YTCs) was targeted to be achieved during 2009-
10. The proposal was placed before the 11th Governi ng Council meeting of MDNIY on the 9th April, 2009.  The action 
taken note does not specify what decision was taken  in the meeting. The proposal was again placed befo re the 12 
Governing Council meeting of MDNIY after a gap of f ull one year, i.e.  on 9th April, 2010 wherein it was decided that 
YTCs may be taken up by the Central Council of Rese arch in YOGA and Naturopathy. The Committee infers from the 
Action Taken Reply that the funds must have been ea rmarked for the purpose, for 2009-10, i.e.  the first target year for 
establishing YTCs and in the absence of concretization of the proposal the budgeted funds must have go t locked up and 
surrendered later on. In the absence of a comprehen sive reply from the Department, the Committee is un able to 
comprehend the reasons behind transferring the YTCs  to CCRYN. Taking all the above factors into accoun t, the 
Committee is constrained to observe that the scarce  resources remained blocked due to delay in approva l and 
indecisiveness on the part of the Department. The C ommittee, therefore, recommends to the Department t o take 
expeditious steps towards realizing targets in respect of YTCs and intimate to it the progress made in this regard.  
       (Para 5.4.3)  
 The Committee would like to be apprised of the fin dings of the Technical Committee constituted to eva luate the 
physical performance of the existing 10 Yoga units and the action taken thereon.   (Para 5.4.4)  
 

VI.  RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT 
 The Committee is not satisfied with the evasive re ply given by the Department. Keeping in view that t here is no 
effective cure/treatment for cancer in the modern s ystem of medicines, the Department should make all out efforts to 
exploit any significant achievement by any system o f medicine towards treatment/cure of such a deadly disease. The 
adequate and effective mechanism should be in place  to expedite scientific validation of any claim in this regard. The 
Committee notes with dismay that the Department has  failed so far in carrying out scientific validatio n of such claims 
due to procedural delays and lack of adequate resea rch work and expertise in this regard. The Committe e would 
reiterate once again that the process of clinical t rial on two claims of cancer needs to start at the earliest. Contention of 
the Department that in the event of any drug being finally marketed, the benefit would be shared by the Council and the 
claimant, does not lead to the ultimate goal of pro viding relief to patients suffering from cancer. It  is a well-known fact 
that this disease is spreading at an alarming rate with new dimensions emerging. In such a scenario, t he Department 
along with the Research Council needs to play a pro-active role.  (Paras 6.6 & 6.7)  
VIII.  NATIONAL MEDICINAL PLANTS BOARD 
 The Committee is not satisfied with the reply of t he Department and would like to be furnished with a Status Note, 
detailing inter-alia  at what level and frequency the matter was taken u p with the State Governments for expediting 
furnishing of UCs and the updated status of UCs and  the amount involved therein. The Committee notes t hat the 
Department has not conveyed the steps taken to addr ess the inherent problem areas hampering the Scheme . The 
Committee observes that the NMPB is mandated to coo rdinate all matters relating to medicinal plants an d support 
policies and programmes for growth of trade, export , conservation and cultivation of medicinal plants.  The Committee 
is also given to understand that the multinationals  are procuring the precious medicinal plants at neg ligible prices and 
exporting them. Since medicinal plants are not only a major resource base for the traditional and alternative health care 
systems but are also a source of livelihood for a l arge segment of our population, the Committee would  like the 
Department to address the issues of growers’ rights , prevention of over-exploitation of medicinal plan ts, protection of 
biodiversity, patent-related issues and determination of fair prices of medicinal plants.   (Para 8.7)  
 The Committee notes that some headway has been mad e towards pilling up the vacant posts in NMPB. However, a 
lot still needs to be done in this direction. The C ommittee, therefore, desires to be apprised of the updated status of 
vacancies and the outcome of efforts made towards filling up of those vacancies.   (Para 8.8)  
 The Committee notes that the Department has detail ed the decisions taken by NMPB in its meeting held on 10th 
July, 2007. However, nothing has been mentioned about the follow-up action taken thereon, though more than three and 
a half years have passed since then. This silence i s all the more baffling in view of the fact that NM PB itself felt in 2007 
that strengthening of State Medicinal Plants Boards is key to proper implementation and monitoring of the project. The 
Department should have acted like a catalyst and en sured forward movement in the matter; instead, it h as chosen to 
remain silent on the issue, which is deplorable. Th e Committee would, therefore, like to be apprised o f the steps taken / 
being taken towards implementing the various decisions taken regarding strengthening of SMPBs.   (Para 8.9)  
IX.   QUALITY CONTROL OF AYUSH DRUGS 
 This is yet another instance of casual reply by th e Department. Instead of furnishing a comprehensive  reply 
detailing the specific measures being taken/contemplated to be taken towards overcoming the shortcomings as identified 
in the mid-term appraisal, the Department has merely made a generic statement which, in the opinion of the Committee, 
is tantamount to being evasive. The Committee, acco rdingly, recommends to the Department to shed more light on the 
measures being taken for addressing the shortcoming s, especially those concerning quality control and quality 
assurance.      (Paras 9.1, 9.2, 9.3,9.4 & 9.5)  
 The Committee is well aware that compliance of lab eling provision on AYUSH drugs as mandated under th e 
Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules made thereu nder is the responsibility of State Drug Licensing Authorities. 
Merely writing to the State Governments in this reg ard from time to time will not ensure the complianc e of this very 
crucial condition. The Committee has been repeatedl y emphasizing the need for having an effective moni toring 

mechanism for quality control of AYUSH drugs both w ith the objective of protecting the consumers’ inte rest as well as 
propagation of this alternative system of medicine.   (Para 9.6)  
X.  AYUSH PHARMACEUTICAL INDUSTRY 
Indian, Medicine Pharmaceutical Corporation Limited (IMPCL) 
 The Committee welcomes the much awaited approval o f the 3rd phase of modernization of the Indian Medi cine 
Pharmaceutical Corporation Limited (IMPCL). The Com mittee hopes that implementation of this project wi ll be 
accomplished in a time-bound manner.   (Para 10.3)  
XI.  DEVELOPMENT OF COMMON FACILITIES FOR THE AYUSH IND USTRY CLUSTERS 
 The Committee is constrained to observe that the r eply of the Department is full of ambiguity. Instea d of 
unraveling various dimensions of under-utilization of the funds in unambiguous terms, the Department h as sought to 
prevaricate. For example, the Committee was earlier  informed by the Department that the allocation of Rs. 25.00 crore 
in BE 2009-10 was brought down to Rs. 10.00 at RE s tage due to reduced allocation as a whole for the D epartment. The 
Department has now informed that allocation had to be reduced to Rs. 10.00 at RE stage due to inadequa te proposals 
received during the 1st half. The Committee would t herefore, like the Department to explain this ambig uity. The 
Committee also notes that against the utilization f igures of Rs. 8.57 crore as on 15th March, 2010, th e funds released 
upto 31st March, 2010 amounted to Rs. 16.54 crore. The Committee would, like the Department to indicat e the 
proposals received for funding under this head and the amount released for them, month-wise.   (Para 11.2)  
XII.  SURVEY ON USAGE AND ACCEPTABILITY OF AYUSII 
 The Department has chosen to remain silent on the issue of how the funds to the tune of Rs. 66 lakhs have been 
spent when no agency was finalised to conduct the survey. The Committee would like to be apprised on this account.  
       (Para 12.3)  
XIII.   DEVELOPMENT OF INSTITUTIONS 
 The Committee observes that modifications in the e ligibility criteria for releasing grants-in-aid to AYUSH 
Educational Institutions is a positive initiative t aken by the Department. The Committee would appreci ate if all the 
procedural formalities for approval of the Scheme are completed at the earliest.   (Para 13.4)  
XV.  INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION 
 The Depart{Dent has not indicated any forward move ment made by the Advisory Committee set up under th e 
Chairmanship of Dr. R.A. Mashelkar. The Committee desires to be kept apprised of the progress made by the Advisory 
Committee.             (Para 15.2)

CHAPTER-I
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT HAVE 
BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE  
II.  BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
Recommendations/Observations  
2.10   Committee’s attention has also been drawn by  unspent balances lying with a number of Institutio ns. As on 1st 
December, 2009, maximum unspent balances amounting to Rs. 28.79 crore, Rs. 36.52 crore and Rs. 80.43 c rore were reported 
against the North-Eastern Indira Gandhi Regional Institute of Health and Medical Sciences, Shillong, LGB Regional Institute of 
Mental Health, Tezpur, Assam and AIIMS, New Delhi. Except AIIMS, the other two Institutes had unspent balances as on 1st 
April, 2009. Reasons for availability of such a hug e amount of unspent balances are not known to the C ommittee. However, 
such a state of affairs in national level institute s is indeed a cause  of concern for the Committee. This clearly shows that some 
major activities both ongoing/proposed might be adv ersely affected. The Committee would appreciate if the matter is taken up 
with the concerned authorities without further delay. 
Action Taken  
  The Department shares the concern of the Hon’ble Committee and has made it clear to the Institutions  concerned that 
further fund releases will depend on the pace of liquidation of their unspent balances. 
Recommendations/Observations  
2.13   The Committee notes that as a further effort  to maximize liquidation of UCs, a communication has been sent by the 
Secretary (Health) to the Principal Health Secretaries of all the States. If need be, this exercise ne eds to be pursued further with 
higher authorities. 
Action Taken  
  A D.O. letter at the level of Secretary (Health) is being issued to all the Chief Secretaries of the  States concerned after 
compilation of State-wise data pertaining to the grants released upto 31.03.2009. 
IV.   SAFDARJUNG  HOSPITAL  AND VARDHMAN MAHAVEER M EDICAL COLLEGE, NEW DELHI 
Recommendations/Observations  
4.2   The Committee notes that against projected Pl an requirement of Rs. 180.60 crore for 2010-11 for the Hospital, allocation 
of Rs. 118.60 crore has been made. Given the fact t hat out of the RE plan allocation of Rs. 129.92 cro re for 2009-10, the 
Hospital was able to spend Rs. 112.76 crore upto 28th February, 2010, with every possibility of full utilization by the end of the 
year, the Committee is unable to comprehend the rea sons behind a huge gap of Rs. 62.00 crore between t he projected and 
budgeted funds for 2010-11. The Committee, therefor e, recommends that additional funds be allocated fo r the Hospital at RE 
stage so that lack of funds should not hamper the re-developmental activities undertaken by the Hospital. 
Action Taken  
  Noted for compliance. 
Recommendations/Observations  
4.12   The Committee is constrained to observe that  the allocated funds for 2009-10 could not be utili zed even after steep 
reduction at the RE stage. To add to this the Depar tment’s reply that the reduction was due to realist ic assessment of the needs 
of the Institute, proves that the earlier estimate,  at the BE stage was not proper. Moreover, the fact  that the College could not 
utilize this reduced amount also makes it clear tha t there is some element of improper planning at som e stage. The Committee, 

accordingly, recommends to the Department to have a realistic assessment of the fund requirement for t he College at the outset 
itself. 
Action Taken  
  The suggestions of the Committee will be complied  with. 
VI.  ALL INDIA INSTITUTE OF MEDICAL SCIENCES (AIIMS ) 
Recommendations/Observations  
6.10  Committee’s attention has been drawn by a ver y disturbing trend of utilization of allocated fund s by AIIMS. Director, 
AIIMS during his deposition before the Committee, informed that during 2008-09 and 2009-10 some Plan Funds were diverted 
to Non-plan for paying the Sixth Pay commission’s a rrears and various other allowances to AIIMS employ ees. As a result, 
development projects could not be taken up. Frequen t changes in the plan projects also had a negative impact. The Committee 
would like to point out that diversion of plan fund s to non-plan side is in direct contravention of fi scal norms. The Committee 
deplores such a development at the premier Institute of the country. It seems that this trend has been  continuing since long. The 
Committee wonders about the role of Internal Audit Wing and Financial Adviser of the Department. The C ommittee is also 
very unhappy with the non-provision of required non-plan funds meant for payment of arrears and allowances to the employees 
which are anticipated beforehand. The Committee wou ld appreciate if fiscal management at AIIMS is brou ght to order. The 
Committee cannot accept the diversion of plan funds  meant for development projects to non-plan side. U rgent action needs to 
be, taken in this crucial matter so that this trend is not allowed to continue any further. 
Action Taken  
  The Institute was allocated Rs.566.00 crore (Non- Plan) and Rs.320.51 crore (Plan) against the requir ement of Rs.636.88 
crore (Non-Plan) and Rs.270.00 crore (Plan). Since there was requirement of Rs.636.88 crore (Non-Plan)  to meet the essential 
requirements of the Institute and to make payment o f arrear according to Sixth Pay Commission and fund  beyond Rs.566.00 
crore could not be provided by the Ministry under Non-Plan, Rs.70.00 crore were re-appropriated by the Ministry from the Plan 
fund. As desired by the Committee, every effort will be made to follow the fiscal discipline. 
VII.   POST GRADUATE INSTITUTE OF MEDICAL EDUCATION  AND RESEARCH (PGIMER),  
  CHANDIGARH  
Recommendations/Observations  
7.3  The Committee is happy to note that during the  first three years of the Eleventh Plan, there has not been a reduction in the 
Plan funds at the RE stage. This is an indication t hat the allocated funds are being fully utilized by  the Institute for its 
developmental activities. 
Action Taken  
  Efforts will continue to be made in this regard. 
X.   LADY HARDINGE MEDICAL COLLEGE AND SMT. SUCHETA  KRIPALANI HOSPITAL,  
  NEW DELHI 
Recommendations/Observations  
10.7  The Committee is very disturbed with the pers isting shortage of staff in the college/hospital un der the Department. The 
Committee recommends to the Department to make all conceivable efforts for an early filling up of the vacant posts so that the 
high standards of patient care are maintained. 
Action Taken  
  The shortage of staff is mainly in the category o f Safai Karmacharis (Group ‘D’ staff)/Clerks. To me et the shortage of 
Safai Karmacharis, the sanitation services are part ially outsourced. Since the appointments against th e Group ‘D’ posts cannot 
be made subsequent to the implementation of the 6th  Pay Commission recommendations, the proposal to pr ovide additional 

Safai Karmacharis by outsourcing is already under c onsideration in consultation with DGHS/the Institut ion concerned. As 
regards Clerks, the Institution has already taken up the matter with the Staff Selection Commission for filling up these posts. 
XIII. PRADHAN MANTRI SWASTHYA SURAKSHA YOJNA (PMSSY) 
Recommendations/Observations  
13.6   After an assessment of the progress of vario us components under the Scheme, the Committee in its 27th Report had 
made its apprehensions very clear that with the way  things were moving, it would take at least another  Plan period before the 
six AIIMS like Institutions would actually start fu nctioning. After a gap of two years, the Committee finds that its 
apprehensions have proved to be correct. It is stil l a distant dream to see these Institutions functio ning. The reason is that even 
after the completion of infrastructure related work , the Department has to concentrate on a whole lot of issues including 
manpower. The Committee would like to point out tha t this ambitious project is of critical importance for creating much 
required tertiary health care facilities in the cou ntry. Under funding of the project should not be al lowed to come in the way of 
access to quality and affordable health care for al l. The Committee, therefore, recommends that higher  level of funds, as 
required, be allocated under this head at RE stage during 2010-11.  
Action Taken  
  The concern of the Committee has been noted by th e Ministry. It is informed that in addition to the action taken as stated 
in Para 13.4, action for manpower planning and finalization of equipments for the six AIIMS-like institutions has been initiated. 
Manpower Committee constituted for finalization of manpower requirement has submitted its report and f urther follow-up 
action like identifying functions/duties, framing recruitment rules etc. is being taken. 
  Considering commencement of work at six AIIMS-lik e institutions, ongoing upgradation projects in the  first phase and 
likely start of second phase upgradation projects, Committee has rightly felt that the allocation of Rs.750 crore for 2010-11 will 
not be sufficient to meet the requirements of vario us activities under the PMSSY and therefore, the fu nd allocation should be 
enhanced to Rs.1500 crore. Steps will be taken at the appropriate time to propose enhanced outlay in RE 2010-11. 
Recommendations/Observations  
13.10   In the opinion of the Committee, the reason s cited for the delay are very flimsy in nature and  indicative of 
ineffectiveness of monitoring and coordination mech anism. The Committee is of the firm opinion that ha d proper coordination 
been done with the concerned agencies of the States  and if the Department had pursued the project vigo rously towards 
achieving the set targets, it could have approached  the State Governments at an appropriately higher l evel to thrash out State 
specific problems. The same is apparently lacking on the part of the Department. 
Action Taken  
  Noted. State Governments have constituted a Proje ct Monitoring Committee under the chairmanship of C hief Secretary, 
comprising of Secretary (Health/Medical Education),  representatives of local bodies/municipal authorit ies, civil works/forest 
departments, District Collector/Police Superintendent etc. in order to monitor the progress of work at  each of the AIIMS sites 
and also to resolve local/site specific issues. Regular meetings of the Committee are being held. 
Recommendations/Observations  
13.15  The Committee also recommends to the Departm ent to start ground work in respect of the issues l ike requirement of 
manpower, machines and equipments etc. so that once  the construction work is complete, no further dela y is caused in the 
operationalisation of the Institutes. 
Action Taken  
  Action for manpower planning for all the six AIIM S-like institutions has been initiated. Technical Committee constituted 
under the chairmanship of Director, PGIMER, Chandig arh worked out requirement of manpower to be recrui ted in phases. 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is in the pro cess of identifying functions and duties and also f raming of recruitment 
rules for each of the posts recommended by the Technical Committee. 
Recommendations/Observations  

13.16 The Committee takes a very serious view of th e persistent non-compliance of an assurance given b y the then Secretary 
during his presentation before the Committee during  examination of Demand for Grants (2008-09) of the Ministry to furnish a 
status report to the Committee regarding implementa tion of PMSSY project after every two months. The p roject is one of the 
landmark initiatives to enable the people of this c ountry across States to have access to quality heal thcare. Further, it involves 
enormous amount of precious tax payer’s money. Ther efore the Committee needs to keep a close watch on the progress of the 
Scheme. The Committee therefore reminds the Departm ent to be careful and keep its assurance given befo re a Parliamentary 
Committee mandated to scrutinize its work. 
Action Taken  
  Noted for compliance. A detailed Note in reply to  para 11.5 of the 27th Report of the Committee for 2008-09 was sent in 
March, 2010. A status report was also sent on 12.5.2010. 
XIV.  DEVELOPMENT OF NURSING SERVICES  
Recommendations/Observations  
14.5   The Committee is not happy with the abnormal  delays in bureaucratic procedures of seeking appro val. However, 
now that the new scheme has got the requisite appro val of the Cabinet, the Committee would recommend t o the Department to 
pursue the various components under the scheme vigo rously. The Committee also recommends to the Depart ment to make a 
realistic assessment of funds requirement for various components and seek more funds at the RE stage.  
Action Taken  
  Noted for compliance. As regards the realistic as sessment of funds, it is stated that the requiremen t is being worked out 
with the involvement of the concerned States and a total of Rs.17.70 crores has been released under va rious components of the 
scheme so far. Necessary funds would also be sought at the RE stage based on requirement. 
Recommendations/Observations  
14.7  The Committee is not prepared to accept the s tand of the Department that for both training and s trengthening of 
institutions proposals have to come from the States . When the Department has started the scheme, and r ightly so as per 
requirement of the profession, it has to take lead and responsibility to make it successful. It should  motivate the nursing 
institutions to come up with proposals to avail the  benefits under the scheme. Mere formal requests do  not make any scheme 
successful. Concerted efforts need to be made by the Department in this regard. 
Action Taken  
  Noted for compliance. Action is being taken. Conc erted efforts are being made for initiating the proposal from States. 
Recommendations/Observations  
14.14  The Committee is of the considered opinion t hat maintaining a Live Register of nurses would be of great help in 
formulating the various policies w. r. t.  the nursing personnel. Accordingly, the Department  needs to take up the issue with all 
the State Councils with some sense of urgency. The Department may also think of some kind of framework  whereby the State 
Councils are persuaded to start maintaining a live register of nurses as also share the details with t he Department to facilitate 
better policy formulation. 
Action Taken  
  Noted for compliance. 
Recommendations/Observations  
14.16  The Committee is very concerned with the sho cking findings of the nursing training programmes i n Bihar, Orissa, 
Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh that ca me into light after the rapid assessment made by WH O, in collaboration 
with Indian Nursing Council. The picture of other States is also stated to be no better. While appreciating the initiative taken by 
the Department, the Committee recommends that a strategy needs to be chalked out whereby institutions getting grants from the 

Department are brought under some kind of regular t raining quality assessment schedule. This would not only help in plugging 
the loopholes but also help in devising better strategy for achieving desired training standards. 
 
Action Taken  
  Noted for compliance. As desired, a strategy will  be worked out. 
XVII. NATIONAL TOBACCO CONTROL PROGRAMME (NTCP)  
Recommendations/Observations  
17.7  The Committee is happy to note that the Depar tment is focusing on Mass Media/IEC campaign to gen erate awareness 
among the common people about the harmful effects of tobacco products. Awareness among the common masses, especially the 
younger generation, is the key to success of the wh ole Programme. The Committee would recommend that e vents like coming 
Commonwealth Games, venues of cricket and other mat ches being played in India, public gathering like t he kumbh melas etc. 
may also be utilized to generate awareness among people with Mass Media/ IEC campaign at the sites. 
Action Taken  
  Mass Media/IEC campaign through Prasar Bharti (Do ordarshan and All India Radio), NFDC and DAVP are b eing aired 
for creating awareness among the common people abou t the harmful effects of tobacco products. During t he Kumbh mela at 
Haridwar, special activities were undertaken for sensitizing about Tobacco Control in collaboration with NGOs. The Ministry is 
also developing “Guideline for Tobacco-free Commonwealth Games” in collaboration with Government of NCT of Delhi. 
XVIII. MEDICAL EDUCATION 
Recommendations/Observations  
18.4  The Committee is not inclined to agree with t he Department’s view that all is well with the exis ting procedure for 
recognition of MBBS degree colleges. The Department  cannot escape from its responsibility by citing th at it is the 
responsibility of the individual colleges to seek r ecognition. The Committee opines that the Departmen t needs to have into 
consideration the psychological impact of such a si tuation on the final year students who in its opini on would be more anxious 
to see their college getting recognition rather than taking their examinations seriously. The Committee is of the considered view 
that the whole procedure of recognition should be c omplete well before the final year students take th eir examinations. The 
Committee therefore recommends to the Department to  revisit its stand on the issue and come up with so me concrete steps. A 
status note on the issue of recognition to 15 medic al colleges where the first batches of MBBS student s have appeared for final 
examination in the academic year 2010 may be furnished. 
Action Taken  
  As per the provisions of MCI Regulations on Estab lishment of medical colleges, permission to establish a medical college 
and admit students is granted initially for a perio d of one year and is renewed on yearly basis subjec t to verification of 
achievements of annual targets. It is the responsibility of the person to apply to the MCI for purpose of renewal six months prior 
to the expiry of the initial permission. The MCI ca rries out inspections for annual renewal of permiss ion till such time the 
establishment of the Medical College and expansion of the hospital facilities are complete and a forma l recognition of the 
medical qualification of the college is granted. 
  The Committee’s view to complete whole procedure of recognition well before the final year student t ake their 
examination is appreciated. It will take some time to review the procedure of recognition as it requir es consultation with 
Medical Council of India. 
  Present status of 15 medical colleges where first  batch of MBBS students has appeared for final examination but are yet to 
be recognized in the academic year 2010 as on 14.5.2010 is at Annexure-XII . 
Recommendations/Observations  

18.7   The Committee is in full agreement with the initiatives proposed by the Dental Council of India (DCI) especially in 
view of the fact that so many seats are lying vacant year after year. Further, the Committee is of the firm opinion that education 
and accordingly the number of seats should be need based and keeping in view the demand and supply sce nario. Here, by the 
figures available with the Committee, it is amply clear that there is an urgent need for intervention to balance the same. In view 
of the above, the Committee recommends to the Depar tment to take some urgent steps in consultation wit h the DCI and the 
various State Governments, so that this unwanted trend is arrested at the earliest and precious resources are utilized purposefully 
in other areas of medical education. The Committee also recommends to the Department to actively consi der the proposal 
submitted to it by the DCI regarding making norms of opening new college more stringent. 
Action Taken  
  The DCI Regulations governing the establishment o f new dental colleges are made stringent and are be ing changed 
suitably viz . 
a.  Essentiality certificate from the State Governm ent with a statement that in case the applicant fai ls to create 
infrastructure for the dental college, fresh admiss ion will be stopped and the State Government shall take over the 
responsibility of the students already admitted in the college with the permission of the Central Government. 
b.  University affiliation from the concerned Unive rsity. 
c.  Attachment with own 100 bedded General Hospital / Government General Hospital/Medical College with a radius 
of 10 kms. 
d.  Accreditation of dental colleges by the externa l agency. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
CHAPTER-II 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN 
VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT’S REPLIES 
II   BUDGETARY  ALLOCATION  
Recommendations/Observations  
2.4   With this trend of allocation of funds and ut ilization thereof, the Committee does not have much  hope about optimum 
release of funds out of the approved outlay of Rs. 41092.92 crore in the remaining two years of the El eventh Plan. The 
Department will have to make concerted efforts so a s to ensure optimum utilization of plan allocation of Rs. 5560.00 crore in 
2010-11. Only then, there are chances of enhanced provision being made in 2011-12, the last year of the Eleventh Plan.  
Action Taken  
  The Department notes the concerns of the Committe e and submits that major hurdles like poor absorpti ve capacity under 
the NRHM and lack of approval of many major schemes  having been removed, there are very good prospects  of larger fund

3.25   Though the Committee appreciates Department’ s initiative for ensuring quality service to CGHS b eneficiaries and 
has no doubts over the professionalism of NABH/NABL , yet it does not find much merit in making it comp ulsory as a 
precondition for empanelment under CGHS. The NABL/N ABH lay down certain norms and standards to be obse rved and on 
inspection, they provide accreditation to those who  fulfil the said standards. There is no guarantee t hat once accredited, the 
Hospital/diagnostic centre will maintain those standards till the next inspection by NABL/NABH. Further, it has been observed 
that many of the reputed hospitals don’t go for acc reditation under them. In such a scenario it may be  counterproductive as the 
beneficiaries may be deprived of services under suc h reputed Hospitals/diagnostic centres. The Committ ee accordingly 
recommends to the Department to be cautious on this move. 
3.26   The Committee would also like to have inform ation regarding the number of NABH/NABL accredited Government 
hospitals/diagnostic centres as well as private hospitals/diagnostic centres empanelled under CGHS. 
Action Taken  
  When the CGHS initiated and completed the process  of empanelment of private hospitals and diagnostic  centres during 
2004, the so called big hospitals acted pricey and did not accept the rates arising out of tender proc ess. CGHS was left with no 
option but to empanel only those hospitals and diag nostic centres which accepted the package rates. CG HS has no power to 
compulsorily empanel hospitals and diagnostic centr es under it. After the completion of empanelment pr ocess, considerable 
doubts were expressed in various forums that CGHS e mpanelled “fly-by night operators” and “big hospita ls have been 
eliminated from the tendering process”. One point that no one appreciated was that CGHS had prescribed the parameters for the 
hospitals and diagnostic centres to fulfil before e mpanelment and also that the empanelment orders wer e not issued without the 
specific recommendation of the Quality Council of I ndia. Quality Council of India (QCI) is an organisa tion set up by the 
Ministry of Commerce and Industry. A team of QCI wo uld physically inspect the premises of the hospital s and diagnostic 
centres to confirm that they conformed to the param eters fixed by the CGHS, and only those hospitals a nd diagnostic centres 
were recommended to the CGHS for empanelment as wer e fulfilling the prescribed conditions. In addition , the hospitals and 
diagnostic centres were required to submit bank guarantees and sign MOA with CGHS, which had stringent conditions. 
  The criticism of CGHS of ignoring “big” hospitals  continues even today though on a slightly muted condition. 
  According to QCI, accreditation is a process base d on a system implemented across the organisation. It has to be practiced 
by its management, staff, clients (patients) all the time and being continuously monitored, leaving no room for relaxation of the 
requirements. Moreover, it is a process adopted by the management with an aim to improve its services.  It is different from an 
inspection which is based on the verification of in frastructure on fixed time basis. Therefore, accred itation mechanism is 
entirely different from the inspection. Accreditati on body also monitors the performance of .its accre dited facilities on a 
continuous basis by way of on-site surveillance ass essments, renewal assessments, off-site monitoring using data on various 
indicators, verifying complaints from users of the services, etc. Thus, a hospital once accredited doe s not mean that it will 
remain accredited forever. NABH can suspend or with draw accreditation on various grounds laid down in its policies and 
known to accredited hospitals. Patient safety and qualify of care are cardinal points in the accreditation. The accredited hospital 
needs to establish systems, processes and more impo rtantly monitor key clinical outcomes. All major gr oups of hospital 
industry, i.e.  Apollo, Fortis, Max Wockhardt, Columbia Asia, Narayana Hrudalaya, etc., have adopted NABH accreditation. 

  Unlike regulation, accreditation is voluntary. Ac creditation is driven by market forces, empanelling  and paying agencies. 
It stands to logic that paying agency has the right  to demand quality and the CGHS has taken the appro priate decision to 
demand accreditation so as to provide safe healthcare to its beneficiaries. 
  Presently, 45 private and 2 Government hospitals have been accredited by NABH and there are over 400  applications for 
accreditation which are under different stages of evaluation for accreditation. Over 70 hospitals have undergone pre-assessment 
and now working towards final assessment. Over 20 h ospitals have undergone final assessment and now wo rking to close the 
deficiencies so that case can be put to the Accredi tation Committee for recommendation. It is a dynami c process and the 
statistics keep changing as hospitals keep moving from one step to another. 
  It is learnt that after the CGHS imposed the cond ition of accreditation with NABH / NABL for empanel ment under it, 
QCI received over 300 applications for accreditation, which proves that private hospitals and diagnostic centres need CGHS for 
their profitability as much as CGHS wants them to s erve its beneficiaries. The condition will, in the long run, prove beneficial 
to the welfare of CGHS beneficiaries, which is a win-win situation for CGHS.

15.8  The Committee is aware that active cooperatio n of the State Governments is key to the success of  a Programme of vast

the Department needs to take a pro-active approach and try to bring all the States on board for effect ive implementation of the 
Programme and have regular interactions with them. It is high time that the problem areas hampering the implementation of the 
Programme are identified and suitable and timely action taken accordingly.

increasing the PG training capacity in mental healt h, provision of training for general health staff i n mental health and a more 
active monitoring and mentoring system for involvin g the states actively. More regular interventions h ave been planned and 
would be intensified further once the dedicated monitoring mechanism is in place.  
Recommendations/Observations  
15.12  Majority of districts in the country have no t still been covered under District Mental Health P rogramme, which was 
initiated way back in 1996. It has taken almost 15 years for extending the component to only 123 distr icts. With about 500

failed to take off so far. With the Secretary herse lf indicating a further delay, the Committee does n ot have hope of more 
districts being covered under this component and of  the Programme in the near future. The Committee, t herefore, recommends 
to the Department to seriously take all conceivable  measures to cover the 200 Districts under DMHP, as  envisaged in the 
Eleventh Plan period.  
Action Taken  
  For the plan period, expansion of DMHP to new dis tricts has not been recommended in view of shortage of funds as well 
as shortage of manpower for the programme. However, all conceivable measures to extend the programme to 200 more districts 
will be explored by the programme division. Eleventh Plan covered 27 districts and Tenth Plan covered 110 districts, achieving 
more than the target of expansion of DMHP to 100 districts.

XVII. NATIONAL TOBACCO CONTROL PROGRAMME (NTCP) 

Recommendations/Observations  
17.2   The Committee is constrained to observe that  in 2007-08 and 2009-10 BE funds had to be revised downwards 
substantially at the RE stage keeping in view the p ace of expenditure under the Programme. Against an allocation of Rs. 40.00 
crore and 30.00 crore in 2007-08 and 2009-10 respectively, an expenditure of only Rs. 13.98 crore and Rs. 16.60 crore has been 
reported. The Committee opines that time and again the Department brings the rhetoric of scarcity of f unds and here it is not 
utilizing the available resources persistently. The  Committee may be informed of the measures taken by  the Department to 
optimally utilize the available resources under this Programme.  
Action Taken  
  The National Tobacco Control Programme was launch ed in 2007-08 as a pilot programme. In the first ye ar (2007-08), 
expenditure incurred under Tobacco Free Initiative was Rs.13.98 crore against RE allocation of Rs.29.0 0 crore. Subsequently, 
in the year 2008-09, actual expenditure was Rs.35.l7 crore against RE allocation of Rs.39.00 crore. Further in the year 2009-10, 
consequent to CCEA approval in January 2010, out of  RE allocation of Rs.17.00 crore, Rs.16.60 crore wa s utilized under the 
National Tobacco Control Programme. 
  A budget allocation of Rs.45.00 crore has been pr ovided under BE 2010-11 under “Tobacco Free Initiatives”. It has been 
decided to carry out the IEC activities under Natio nal Tobacco Control Programme in four phases to uti lize the budget 
allocation of Rs.23.00 crore in the year 2010-11. An amount of Rs.8.00 crore has already been sanctioned so far for running anti 
tobacco campaign through print and electronic Media  in the first phase of campaign during the month of  May-June, 2010. 
Second phase will be initiated after evaluation of the first phase in the month of August-September, 2010. 
  An amount of Rs.14.84 lakhs has been released dur ing the current FY 2010-11 to State Health Society,  Nagaland for 
carrying out NTCP. Further, State and District Toba cco Control Cells are being asked to furnish the ut ilization certificates in 
respect of grants released to them for carrying out  the National Tobacco Control Programme to enable t his Ministry to release 
next instalment of grant to them for the purpose. 
  An amount of Rs.91.00 lakhs has been released dur ing the current FY 2010-11 to IIPS, Mumbai for carr ying out GATS-
India survey and the remaining instalments will be released after the final report is submitted. 
  The process to procure equipment for setting up o f tobacco testing laboratories has been initiated. 
Recommendations/Observations  
17.9   The Committee notes that though the Departme nt has been able to come up with a law for restricting use and sale of 
the Tobacco products, the ground realities have not changed much. The various provisions of the Act are not being implemented 
in letter and spirit even in metro cities in India.  Situation in respect of small towns and rural area s can well be imagined. The 
Department cannot remain a silent spectator on such  vital issues. A proper pro-active strategy should be developed whereby all 
the States are roped in to work sincerely in this regard. 
Action Taken  
  Since the State Governments/ UTs are the main enf orcing agencies for implementing provisions of the Cigarettes and 
Other Tobacco Products (Prohibition of Advertisemen t and Regulation of Trade and Commerce, Production,  Supply and 
Distribution) Act (COTP A), 2003, they have been as ked to ensure strict compliance of the various prov isions of the Act and 
Rules made thereunder. For regular monitoring of th e progress of implementation of the tobacco control  programme, action 
taken reports are sought from the states. 
  Further, Central Level Steering Committees for lo oking into violation of section 5 of the COTP A has  been constituted. 
An Inter-Ministerial task force has been constituted to look at inter-sectoral issues on tobacco control.

XXI.  MISCELLANEOUS 
Recommendations/Observations  
21.4   The Committee is happy with the introduction  of such a policy tendering monetary award to infor mers providing 
information about the spurious drugs. The Committee  would like to be apprised of the details of the po licy along with any 
achievement made so far under the policy.  
Action Taken  
  Whistle Blower Scheme ––  Whistle Blower Scheme has been devised by the cent ral Government for giving monetary 
rewards to the Whistle Blower who can take risk of providing the information about the perpetrators fo r such crimes. The 
Reward scheme provides for giving handsome rewards to the informers who provides specific information to the designated 
authorities leading to the seizures of spurious, adulterated, misbranded and not of standard quality drugs, cosmetics and medical 
devices. This reward scheme will be applicable to both the informers as well as the officers of the Government and CDSCO. 
  The Additional secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has issued letters to all Chief Secr etaries of States/UTs 
on 14th October 2009 with the request for the wide publicity of the Scheme. 
  As per the Whistle Blower Policy, the reward of m aximum of upto 20% of the total cost of consignment s seized will be 
payable to the informer / officials which should no t in any case exceed Rs.25 Lakh in each case. 25% o f the amount will be 
payable to the whistle blower at the time of filing  of complaint in the court of law, 25% at the time of disposal of the case in 
favour of the Government and the rest of the amount, that is, 50% when the case is finally decided and the matter is not pending 
in any court of law in the country. The eligibility  of the informer and the quantum of cash rewards wo uld be decided by a 
Committee, which will consist of officials from different departments / offices. To ensure speedy trials of the cases, these cases 
will be filed before the Designated / Special Court s set up for the purposes of drugs related issues a s per the provisions of the 
Drugs and Cosmetics (Amendment) Act, 2008. 
  Drug Controller General (India) along with other officials will be the nodal authority who will inter alia  oversee the 
functioning of the Reward Scheme as proposed herein above. 
  The Zonal and Sub-Zonal officers of the CDSCO wil l act as the nodal officer to whom the whistle blow er/informer can 
provide the information about the manufacture /movement of spurious /adultered drugs. 
  The identity of the whistle blower/informer will be kept secret and will be known only to the Nodal Officers, i.e. 
concerned zonal and sub-zonal officers of the CDSCO , the DCG (1) and the Director General Health Servi ces. It will be the 
responsibility of the concerned officials to keep the details of the whistle blower / informer secret. 
  On receipt of the information from a whistle blow er/informer, the concerned Nodal officers will orga nize immediate and 
systematic investigation in co-ordination with the State Drugs Control Administration to unearth the spurious drugs racket. 
  The details of the investigations will then be fo rwarded by the concerned zonal/sub-zonal officer to  the DCG (I) for the 
consideration of the committee to decide about the merit of the case for reward and the quantum of rew ard to be given to the 
whistle blower / informer. 
  The CDSCO has received so far 27 cases from the d ifferent parts of the country, however in some case s complaints were 
repeated as they were received twice and some of the cases were found to be fictitious, Rest of the cases are under investigation. 

The details of the current status on the Whistle Bl ower Policy as on 30th April 2010 are at Annexure-XVI  for your kind 
perusal. 
  No reward under the scheme has been offered as th e first instalment has to be given after launching of prosecution in the 
court of Law.

3.9   The Committee views the introduction of the c urrent proposal of the Ministry with serious concern. The Committee is not 
convinced by Department’s categorical statement that it does not intend to replace the CGHS with this new insurance scheme. It 
is amply clear that the scheme would be mandatory f or future employees and pensioners. The Committee w ould like to point 
out that CGHS is one of the very important social s ecurity measures which has been providing health ca re services at 
economical rates to its beneficiaries for so many decades. The Committee fails to comprehend the rationale for depriving all the 
beneficiaries of such an essential service in the l ong run. The Committee would like to point out that  there is a well-structured 
set up of CGHS dispensaries, Government Hospitals p roviding allopathic and AYUSH healthcare and also a  number of 
empanelled diagnostic centres and private hospitals . In the recent years a number of initiatives have also been taken for 

strengthening/revamping different components under the Scheme. A number of additional dispensaries are  also proposed to be 
set up in the near future. The existing CGHS scheme  is part of the social responsibility of government  for its serving/retired 
employees. Full reimbursement as per the prescribed  norms is payable to the beneficiaries. There is no  upper limit on annual 
expenditure on the treatment of a beneficiary. The very idea of capping the amount of coverage to Rs. 5 lakh per family per year 
as well as the limit of coverage to only - Self, sp ouse, two dependent children and dependent parents and thereby forcing for 
payment of the fixed percentage of premium per additional dependent family member under the proposed scheme indicates that 
the Government intends to dilute its social obligation primarily to its employees. This is unacceptable to the Committee. 
Action Taken  
  The proposed health insurance scheme is primarily  aimed at Central Government pensioners residing in areas not covered 
by the CGHS and also for serving Central Government  employees presently not covered by the CGHS. Exist ing CGHS 
beneficiaries will have the option of continuing wi th the CGHS or opt for the proposed health insuranc e scheme, when 
introduced. 
  Additionally, the cost of running the CGHS in the  existing 25 cities has been increasing alarmingly and the Government is 
finding it difficult to fund the increasing need of  funds to maintain the present level of satisfactio n. Presently, CGHS 
beneficiaries are reimbursed their expenditure base d on the package rates fixed for different treatmen t in private hospitals and 
diagnostic centres. Here also, differential entitlement of wards exists. 
  As per information available from IRDA, more than  97% of the claims settled under different mediclaim/health insurance 
policies were claims under Rs.3.00 lakhs; and 0.35%  of the claims were between Rs. 3.00 lakhs and Rs.5 .00 lakhs and the 
balance were over Rs. 5.00 lakhs. Hence, the present proposed coverage of upto Rs. 5.00 lakhs per beneficiary per annum would 
be more than adequate to cover the health needs of the beneficiaries who would be joining the health insurance scheme. 
  It is not that the beneficiaries would be left hi gh and dry if the expenditure exceeded RS.5.00 lakns in any given year. The 
proposal includes a provision for the creation of c orpus for reimbursement of expenditure beyond the a nnual limit of Rs. 5.00 
lakhs, on a case to case basis. What is being propo sed in the scheme is that the liability of the insu rance agency would be upto 
the limit of Rs.5.00 lakhs. 
  In order to encourage small family norms, it is p roposed to restrict the number of persons to be cov ered under the 
proposed scheme. It is denied that the Government i s diluting its social obligation primarily to its e mployees. The proposed 
scheme allows the coverage of self, spouse, two dependent children and dependent parents, which clearly shows that the benefit 
is sought to be extended to the nearest family members of the beneficiary. 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE  
  The Action Taken Note furnished by the Department h as proved beyond doubt the apprehensions of the 
Committee that the Government wants to dilute its s ocial obligation towards its employees. The justifi cation by the 
Department that the proposed health insurance schem e is primarily aimed at Central Government pensione rs residing 
in the areas not covered by the CGHS and also for t he serving Central Government employees presently not covered by 
the CGHS, does not hold ground as it would be manda tory for the new entrants in Government service apd  those 
retiring subsequent to its introduction. Further, t he justification that the capping is a well thought  out exercise and 
would be more than adequate to cover the health needs of the beneficiaries is not convincing at all. To prove its point the 
Department has even stated that a provision for the  creation of corpus for reimbursement of expenditur e beyond the 
annual limit of Rs.5.00 lakhs, on a case to case ba sis, is also a part of the scheme. The Committee fi nds this very 
intriguing that when it is ready to shell out reimb ursement over and above this limit, why the limit h as been prescribed 
at all for the beneficiaries. It is understandable that the Department needs to place a capping while negotiating with an 
insurance agency, but keeping discretion of Departm ent to reimburse amount over and above this amount on a case to 
case basis dilutes the responsibility of the Depart ment and can lead to favouritism or even corruption . Another major 
concern is that whether the Insurance agency with w hich the Government is proposing to reach a tie up would promote 
cashless facilities with beneficiaries. The Committ ee has serious apprehensions about the adequacy of this scheme. The 
Committee, accordingly, outrightly rejects the forc ed enforcement of the proposed Insurance Scheme to Government 

servants and recommends to the Department to concen trate on strengthening this well structured CGHS sc heme and 
continue to fulfil Government’s social obligation towards its employees.

3.28  The Committee would like to point out that pr ior to 2001, all the premier specialized hospitals had opted for CGHS 
empanelment. The Committee wonders as to whether th e recently empanelled hospitals of Delhi can provid e the same services 
as being provided by Rajiv Gandhi Cancer Hospital o r Dharamshila Cancer Hospital. The Committee is als o not aware about 
the quality status of the only empanelled hospital.  The Committee reiterates that the kind of speciali zed services being offered 
by a particular hospital, specially for terminal di seases like cancer and not the lowest rates should be the basic criteria for 
selection of a hospital. One must not forget that t he main objective of CGHS is to provide quality hea lth care at economical 
rates. Not only this, Government is supposed to rei mburse only the packages rates. Payment of differen ce in treatment 
expenditure is the concern of the beneficiary. In C ommittee’s view, package rates need to be governed by quality service. 
Nobody stops the concerned authorities to negotiate  with the applicant hospitals for arriving at mutua lly acceptable package 
rates. It cannot be that services offered by a smal l hospital can be considered on an equal footing wi th an advanced well 
established hospital. The Committee, accordingly, recommends framing of a policy for revision of rates after every two years to 
realistically fix the rates of treatment. The Committee may be informed about the action taken by the Department in this regard.  
Action Taken

course. In exceptional cases, negotiation may take place about price/rate alone, and that too with the  lowest responsive bidder

valid for a period of two years with option to cont inue the same for one more year with mutual consent , and thereafter, action 
would be initiated for revision of package rates by floating of fresh tenders.

Recommendations/Observations

not seem to be able to utilize the earmarked funds for the Plan period during the first three years of the Plan period. The Institute 
has been able to utilize only Rs. 648.00 crore (as on 28-2-2010). The Committee sees little hope for o ptimum utilization of 
remaining funds during the last two years of Eleven th Plan. As a result, the initiatives/ongoing proje cts are not likely to be 
executed as targeted originally. The Committee observes that as many as 21 projects were envisaged to be completed during the 
Eleventh Plan for which an outlay of Rs. 623.63 crore was made. The Committee is, however, dismayed to note that by the end

Recommendations/Observations
